title: Coping with consequences of a dog bite before buying a puppy
body:
During our visit to the breeder, my daughter (8) was lightly bitten in the face by the mother dog (a certified Golden Retriever). It happened very unexpectedly; the dog had previously shown herself to be very friendly. The lip bled a bit, and there were long, superficial scratches on the nose. My daughter is brave, but the parents are somewhat frightened and unsettled by the injury to their child before their eyes and the experience of losing control.

What is the correct responsible behavior for the parents? The daughter is very keen on having a dog, but the parents have learned that dogs can be unpredictable. Is this part of the "residual risk" that comes with having a dog?

title: Older brother licking younger sister's legs
body:
Girlfriend and I have a daughter (will be 2 soon), and she has a son (7 turning 8 soon) from a previous marriage. Recently we have been butting heads a lot concerning a few behaviors of son towards daughter, and my reactions to them. One behavior in particular is son's continuing to touch daughter when she is yelling or crying for him to stop (usually she will yell 'no' repeatly, swing her arm at him, or try to push him away; given the size difference and her level of language skills, this is all she can do), and when being told by myself or by mother to leave her alone.

Most recently there was an incident where daughter was lying on pillow in bed in her diaper, and son came in and got on bed and started messing with her. She was relaxing and didn't want to be bothered, so as frequently happens, she started saying no and trying to push him away from her. I didn't say anything immediately, because as mentioned, it is a frequent source of family discord, so I try to choose my battles. He then stuck out his tongue and began to lick her leg, between the knee and the hip, at which point I immediately firmly told him to stop and that he should not do that.

Shortly after, when mother was back in the room, I brought it up with her and asked her to have a conversation with him, because I considered it inappropriate. She got angry at me and told me I only thought it was inappropriate because he was not my son, that if he was my son I would not have a problem with it; and because I was raised by strict, religious, prudish parents (which is true, although I have not been religious myself for decades now, and don't feel that I am prudish).

My question is basically, is it normal or okay for a boy of that age to be licking his younger sister like that? Does it warrant a conversation with him about boundaries, respecting personal space and the desire to be left alone/not touched; or is it better to just ignore? Is it something that most parents would be comfortable with, and am I out of line being bothered by it?

title: How do you reduce the anger a mother feels towards her child?
body:
I met a woman and things have been going well. Recently she has introduced me to her family (older sister and a niece). Her older sister is a widow.

Over the past couple of months, I've grown quite fond of the niece. We have emotionally bonded with each other. She clearly needs a father figure in her life and to be honest, I would not mind being that (it's all very healthy.) In all honesty, the two of us are fulfilling certain emotional needs in each other.

The girl is very nice with me, but with her mother it's different. She keeps on defying her to get a rise out of her (it's working). Here it is winter, and this weekend the child asked her mother if she could go swimming. Her mother told her no, because going swimming in the winter is a bad idea, and she decided to jump in the pool anyway.

The mother started yelling at the child; she had a true meltdown. I have never seen a woman that angry before.

I look at the child and see just how much pleasure the response she is getting gives her. I pulled her out of the swimming pool and told her to go to her room. After a few moments, the mom calmed down.

You have already lost one parent and now you make your mother so angry that you risk losing another. If those school teachers of yours see one thing that leads them to suspect abuse in the house they are obligated by law to report it. You think the social worker will not take you away?

She starts crying and I tell her I don't want to hear it. I then tell her that I do intend to eventually marry into this family and I won't allow her to ruin it for me.

The thing is I'm a 35 year old bachelor that is having this parental role thrust on me. The mother should just have it go. If you give a child such control over your emotions, they will abuse it.

Luckily I was present to de-escelate the situation but I won't always be there to do so. How do I convince her to not spank angrily?

title: 3 Year Old Son - Only Interested in “Girl” Things
body:
My 2, almost 3, year old son is only interested in “girl” activities and play items. He has an older brother, who had no interest in this type of play so our house is mostly neutral or “boy” toys.

My son loves jewelry, makeup, dresses, hair, princesses, the color pink etc.

For now, I act interested in what he likes and I support him. No shaming in this home.

This isn’t a post to ask what should do, or how to treat him. However, I’m curious, if anyone else has had a similar experience with their child at a young age and if their interests changed or if it stayed the same as an older child. I’ve read that this age is too young to come to any conclusions regarding gender or sexuality but I am curious on real life examples. If you’re comfortable sharing please do. Thank you.

title: How to prepare children for evil
body:
I want to prepare my children for life in the best possible way (as most parents do), and an important aspect of this is, in my opinion, teaching them about the evil things humans are capable of, so that they can look for signs and try to avoid or fight it. Maybe the classic teaching in this regard is "don't take anything from strangers, don't go with them, no matter how nice they seem". But this does not tell the child what the problem really is. I believe the child is better prepared if they know what could happen if they followed the stranger. So the child should know about for example: rape, torture, drug addiction, violence because of differing sexual orientation or religion... to name a few. But they shouldn't be so terrified that they cannot function properly (like feeling the need to run away whenever a stranger talks to them).

I do think they should confront all those horrors (by reading, watching films, talking about it) in order to be prepared, but I don't know when and in what dosage. I don't want to turn them into psychic wrecks that are too afraid to leave the house, after all.

I am looking for guidelines on how to determine which kind of atrocities my child can mentally handle, and in what way (at their age or current developmental stage). Are there any parenting books on this? Or any other resources?

For movies, there are age recommendations. And the people who give out these recommendations must have some basis for their decisions. What is that basis?

To give a concrete example where I want to teach but don't know how: I have a 5 year old son. We recently listened to a happy-go-lucky children's podcast episode that was about love and affection and that two people of the same sex being affectionate towards each other is as OK as the standard male-female affection. And in the podcast it was said that "some people do not know this yet, they think only male-female is OK, so we should tell them: love is for everyone!". As if homophobia was just missing knowledge like illiteracy... My take on this is: Sure, there are people - mainly kids - who think it is not OK because they have been told so, but not reflected it in any way. But there are also many people who have CHOSEN to find it not OK, and among them still enough to readily use violence against not only those who are homosexual but also against those who promote accepting homosexuality as OK. And I want my son to know this, so that he does not run around happily-go-luckily, being blind to the evil in humans, telling men who are busy throwing gay couples from roofs that they just haven't heard the news yet. Because he will be next. (Some might argue that the topic of homosexuality is not appropriate for a 5 year old and I tend to agree, but it is impossible - at least for me - to check every bit of media before I expose him to it (especially when I found a series to be suitable, I do not pre-watch/listen every episode), just like I cannot plan every step of his life. So at some point he will be confronted with something new, challenging, disturbing. That's why I am asking this question.)

title: 2 y/o with speech delay
body:
My son turned 2 in April. He is currently in early intervention for speech, they also are working on his receptive language.

When he was 10 months old he got ear tubes after having ear infections for several months. After his tubes were placed we felt like he stopped responding to us, when we called his name or yelled he wouldn’t look. We were concerned about his hearing for several months following the surgery and he couldn’t get through the first hearing test he had but was able to pass at his 2 year appointment. The ear doctor said that his ear infections and tubes had nothing to do with him not speaking but I truly felt that there was a clear difference after his surgery and when they did a pressure test on his ears at 16 months it seemed to correct the problem as he was way more responsive to us but still only saying minimal words.

Well now we have been doing EI for almost 6 months, he has developed a few more words and signs and it’s more consistent with showing us what he wants. He loves to play with his sister and cousins and seeks out other kids when we go to play group or the park. Our EI therapist said she would like to see him be more reactive to her calling his name and for him to do more imitation play although he does it with us. He also gets hyper focused on a toy or activity he is playing and will ignore you if you try to get him to do a different task or activity which I feel is a typical for some toddlers but seems to concern our EI therapist . She has also suggested having him tested for autism but we feel he is too young and everyone who meets him who understands autism or has worked with kids with autism feel that he doesn’t show the typical signs. I should add that he makes eye contact, interacts with other kids and adults that he knows well or even has only met a few times, he also is entering the two year old tantrum stage but it never lasts over 5 minutes if that and he is redirectable.

I am curious peoples thoughts on waiting for testing or giving him more time to develop. He is also starting daycare in a few weeks which will be two full days every week. I just feel there is so much pressure to label kids and it’s becoming very overwhelming for my husband and myself as we do all the suggestions given to us and have seen progress but wish he was saying more. Thank you for any suggestions or words of encouragement.

title: Four Year Old Pushing and Positive Discipline Techniques
body:
This isn't a major problem for us, but I'm curious to get a few perspectives on this issue. My wife and I have two boys, two and four, both close to two and four, and for the most part we try to use positive discipline techniques to correct their behavior. So far we don't really punish them, although we'll very occasionally raise our voice in a targeted way (usually only for the four year old at this point). We try to teach and mentor them into better behavior, rather than making them feel bad about things they've done.

I think, for the most part, this has been successful and we've seen real improvements in self regulation in the four year old. He's very independent, and I would call him mature for his age. The two year old is too young to see much difference.

However, occasionally the four year old will do something a little over the line like push younger brother completely unprompted, and in his last months at daycare he's really starting to test the educators. This is where the question comes in. A part of me thinks: this is all age appropriate for the most part, and he'll gradually grow out of it in the next few years. But he is becoming a little more brazen, and you can tell that he's becoming comfortable testing boundaries because there are no real repercussions to his behavior. For the most part he's well behaved, but when he wants to break a rule he'll break a rule.

So then that leads to the question: do we introduce some kind of mild deterrent to encourage him to stop doing things like pushing his brother, or other ridiculous / dangerous stuff. Something like no TV for the night. Would that kind of thing be age appropriate, or does his behavior come down to not having the ability to fully self regulate?

title: 1.5 year old boy, doesn't seem fully connected socially, compared to his social butterfly outgoing twin brother
body:
I have been worried that my 1.5 year old son is possibly on the autism spectrum. He is. twin so unfortunately I do compare the two. However, it is usually a one way compare, why is he not acting or doing what his brother is?

My son is very laid back, he does have bursts of energy like any kid but most of the time seems in a great mood, happy and content with anything going on. He is verbal and can talk in nearly full sentences, his short sentences are great and spoken correctly although sometimes long sentences/conversations he tries to have could be labeled as gibberish, but it does make sense and is almost always appropriate to the situation. If that makes sense? He can essentially ask for example ( He wonders about his papa tractor and its horn and likes to tell me that its at his papas house) He will say something like " Papas beep beep (tractor) gibberish gibberish at home, papa at home? beep beep. " He will tell you this with great concern for where his papas tractor is at. He when he asks questions gibberish added or not he will have it backed with the correct emotion. "where's sissy?" he will hold his hands out and look at you for an answer. He is hard to make consistent eye contact with, he will some of the time but it is not held long. He has no problem continuing the interaction without eye contact. This has been the ultimate RED FLAG for me, this is what initiated our visit to the peds. He is being seen my Early On, but I they are not assessing him other than once a month visit where they come play with him.

He knows so many words, he knows how most things work. He can work the TV, when the next episode needs to be selected. He doesn't seem to have any sensory issues, if anyone has issues with sensory it's his twin brother, that boy cant stand pants or long sleeve shirts.

There's just something about him that seems off to me, tonight we went to the fair. His brother was so excited for the animals, saying bye bye to them by name, saying hi. Telling his "Nana horse" where his brother in question had no interest in interacting with the animals. He doesn't say hi to strangers like his sister and brother do. Tonight he took a lot of coaxing to get involved and engaged and it honestly broke my heart to see him just not care interact with us, unless we were trying extremely hard, like having to tickle him to get him to become involved. He honestly just loves to walk and wanted nothing but to walk and run around which made him upset multiple times.

He does play with his brother and sister, they parallel play and play together. He will present to sleep and snore, he had a stuff animal cat the other day and was pretending it was running alone the couch and floor meowing the entire time. He will hug the stuff animals and mimic the things they should do. He will copy our dogs and things we say. He will interact with Mickey Mouse clubhouse, sing the theme song and look to you at certain parts because those are his fav. He will follow directions and complete tasks with effort on our part but what 1.5 year old doesn't need help completing tasks asked of them like throwing their dirty diapers away in kitchen garbage that is located in a cabinet that they have to open.

I just cant let it do, he isn't as animated as his siblings. Hes just different from them. I totally know no two children are the same but has anyone else had a child that just constantly teetered on being autistic or not?

title: My parents are getting a divorce how do I prevent it if I am the cause?
body: So I play a sport and I am a state player for the past four years, I have always been on and off badminton while going through thick and thin with my sisters and family . Every time I do something wrong, my whole family gets scolded And I have to live with that thought that I’m the cause of everyone’s misery . My mother (especially)gets scolded for whether it’s not giving me proper nutrition or not enough sleep .my dad is very very ambitious and is very supportive but he gets worked up and hits people when things aren’t his way . My mom just absorbs the pain and takes all the negativity in .. My dad really wants me to be an Olympic Champion. I’m not saying I don’t want to be a champion.. I have the body the height and the money and support from my family … I am also trying my best . recently My dad hired a personal caretaker to take care of me to manage my badminton schedule and train me.. but recently the caretaker brought his family over from another state which angers my dad since he is putting less effort and less time so that he can spend more time with his family . I understand since my dad is paying him 500 per day for a month and he is spending around 3 hours a day only and his cost monthly is around 15,000 ( people in my country earn a average 3000-5000per month ) . And my dad thinks he is doing it for the money and it is good money but I can assure you that it is not for the money . Since he is pretty well off and has 4 successful sons . title: In positive education, what phrase follows the emotional validation?
body:
I’m watching a course on positive parenting and secure attachment, where the instructor emphasizes the importance of "validating the child’s emotions." As an example, they mention a situation where the child wants to have ice cream for breakfast, and after denying it, our job as parents "is not to avoid their frustration, but to acknowledge it." So, what we need to do is maintain boundaries and then empathize by saying things like "I know you were really looking forward to that ice cream" or "You’re feeling a bit disappointed."

When I was a child, the conversation would have been "You can’t have ice cream for breakfast," followed by "because I said so" or "just because." Then, the older family members from my generation, like cousins who now have kids aged 8-10, would say "You can’t have ice cream for breakfast," followed by a lengthy attempt to reason with the child, "because it’s not healthy," "because you already have your cereal," etc.

My question is, exactly following the positive parenting methodology and the approach recommended by the course instructor, how does the conversation continue after the phrases that validate emotions? What exactly follows after "I know you were really looking forward to that ice cream"?

title: Seeming contradiction with respect to selective attention in preschoolers
body:
I can't seem to make sense of a seeming contradiction between scientific research and my observation:

When my preschooler is watching a beetle or my 7-year old is playing Nintendo Switch and I say something, anything, really, the response is zero. I am invisible / non-existent.

Research on the other hand claims that kids have short attention spans and generally don't do selective attention but take in all information.

So why is it that I can't break my kids' focus? Why do they become so focussed and engrossed that they don't hear me even though they are supposed to have a short attention span and bad focussing skills?

Is there any research on this and if so, could someone please point me to it?

title: How to handle excessive self pity
body:
Sometimes my 11 year-old child will fall to excessive self pity. Two examples:

He was very angry about something and tossed away his phone, a corner of the phone cracked and he thought he had broken it completely and permanently. I heard him wailing from the street 200 meters away. I thought something terrible had happed, like maybe he fell and seriously injured himself. His frustration is perfectly understandable: he was already frustrated and then he lost his temper and thought he broke his favourite and most expensive play-thing. But he actively fuels the fire, the crying goes on when all the tears are spent, in a theatrical manner. He throws himself on the couch, grinds his teeth, balls his fists.

Another example: The teacher gaves us exercises to practice writing and spelling at home to help speed up his writing. He hates doing this because its school-work outside school and unlike regular homework this is not something the whole class has to do. He procastrinates, laments how unfair it is he has to do this while his friends don't, then claims he cannot spell and will do everything wrong anyway. He then cries, holds the pencil limply in his hand. While focussing on making a theater and arguing with parents he will make silly mistakes, like not finishing a word or forgetting letters, this fuels more crying and 'see I can't do this'. Last time he was hitting himself in the head with both fists after spending almost 1 hour on writing down two sentences and 5 words.

Again, this is a frustrating situation, but he is making it so much worse. The task is intended to last 15 minutes. I understand I should avoid these situations and help him deal with frustrations but sometimes frustrating things happen. I have read 'How to talk to kids' and I try not to tell him off for his feelings, but I do want him to stop fanning the flames of negative emotions.

title: Walk or Drive to school?
body:
In Greece I see many (not as many as I see in Japanese movies) elementary school kids (6-12) walking on their own to their school. I myself almost always got drived to school (my parents never walked me to school). I only regularly walked myself to school in highschool (I was 14 because I was born in December). I am interested and curious about parental choices (maybe my parents could have done better, I am close to parenting age, seeing young children on the road leaves me wondering).

What should you do with your kids when the distance to school is less than a mile or two? Assume a relatively safe area when it comes to crimes, a slight uphill slope ~100 metres, and some navigation problems and risks of traffic accidents. How does this choice change as they grow older (probably they gain navigation skills, independence, can better manage their wake-sleep cycles)?

The options I see are three:

  1. Walk them there
  2. Send them off on their own
  3. Drive them to school

Walking has the benefit of freedom of motion. (Driving a mile or two with heavy traffic is not the best thing and is unpredictable; half an hour on foot is usually half an hour while a 5-minute drive can become 15-20.) If they walk on their own they gain independence and might socialize on their way there. (It also saves you time to leave for work in the morning but the main focus is parenting.) If their parents walk them there that is safer (especially at younger ages with traffic accidents) and that is some quality time spent with the kids.

Driving can save some minutes of (their) sleep especially in the morning (unless there is a lot of traffic or you can't find a place to park).

title: How to help 13 year old to be more open, motivated and responsible
body:
I have a son - 13 yrs old. He is doing well in his school gifted in both Math and Language arts. But he has a few behavioral / personality issues that seem to be bothering us especially now since he is reaching his puberty age and looking for more independence.

  1. He is not particularly strong willed. He tried a few things and giving up as soon as he think it is too hard for him. For ex. I enrolled him in karate class at the age of 6, he reached very close to black belt but now left it since he is finding it too hard.
  2. He is too picky in eating, small for his age and he seems to have accepted it that he is different from his peers but at the same time he also feels inferior that he is small and not as strongly built as his peers.
  3. He is not physically too active, he likes to lie around play games or watch vidoes from his favorite youtube channel and gets less involved in physical activities. To motivate him, we got a table tennis table, pickle ball set, swimming twice a week, tennis classes, badminton etc. And I encourage him to come join with me and his younger brother playing these games and other board games and family activities but none of these interests him.
  4. Till now he used to read a lot but now he also lost interest in reading.
  5. The biggest issue now I am facing is he is not motivated to do anything. He has in front of him his 2 yr younger brother who is so much into trying all sorts of things, trying all kinds of technical things including building his own gaming PC, building custom RC cars, trying all kinds of other STEM experiments his age. I am mentioning his younger brother not to compare both of them but just that his yonger brothers example in front of him doesnt work to motivate him. However whatever little he helped his yonger brother do his stuff, he is quick to take credit for what he did.
  6. He doesnt have friends his age, he talks and likes to hang around with his younger brothers friends. This might be linked to the point 2 above.
  7. He has strong attitude problem which is why he is not a type someone would like to be aroud with. Very quick to blame others for something wrong that happened with him, not willing to take responsibility for his own choices. Likes to argue when you try to talk to him about what he needs to work on or improve upon. Recently his tennis coach complained that he tried to talk to him about what he needs to improve upon, but instead of working on his mistake he argued about what his coach did wrong.
  8. Clumsy. I have to keep reminding him about tying his shoe laces, brushing his teeth, combing his hairs, cleaning his room etc. He is very forgetful and keeps missing his basic chores.

Things I do as his dad -

  1. I spend a lot of time with him take him to swimming, tennis, frisby, badminton etc. Also play family board games, chess and ping-pong.
  2. I read a lot, about 2-3 hours a day as a hobby, and I think it may motivate him to restart his reading.
  3. I talk a lot about making healthier eating choices, making better overall/holistic life-style choices.
  4. We always have meals together and I initiate discussion about how he is doing at school, whether he needs any help at anything and a bunch of other family fun/silly talks.

Inspite of all negative points I mentioned in the previous section, one thing never to forget is he is very gentle, sweet and innocent child when all is going well. Very willing to help others with what he is good at. And I as his dad can relate to all those things mentioned above since I was and still am pretty much the same personality. I hit my maturity age pretty late at around 20-22 yrs and I know no one liked to be around me in my childhood, I learnt my lessons a hard/ugly and painful way and tried to improve upon a bunch of those things which can make me hard to be with. I know he is just following me, but I just want to see if there is any better way he can learn his lessons, get motivated, be more open to try new things. I could be doing certain things wrong which is triggering a few of these issues and looking for some suggestions about what I can do to help him grow well.

Please help!

title: How to navigate a 2 year old saying "stop it" to everyone
body:
My almost 2 year old has just entered the "mine" stage and is having a hard time sharing toys and taking turns. I understand this is developmentally appropriate for her age and explain turn taking and such to her each time we hear "No, mine."

Recently however I told her when she wants daddy to stop tickling her she should say "Stop" or "Stop it" instead of the usual "No!"

This worked well for the games but now she will tell anyone to "Stop it!" When they walk into a room, if they're on a toy she wanted to use, literally anything and all day long.

How should I approach this?

I have been redirecting her when I can, trying to provide more words for what she's saying.

I will say things like "No, she is doing cooking right now and can't stop. What can you see her cooking?" Or "They are using the slide right now and you would like a turn? Let's wait here for our turn."

Does anyone have any advice?

I've had some family member complain that it's rude and while it does feel that way I know it is just her learning how to use those words and in what context. Expanding on her sense of self. Experimenting with what she can control.

I don't want to make it worse or solidify her use of the words but I also want her to know she can tell someone to stop touching her for example

title: Is time really the only solution for a child with attachment issues?
body:
My partner and I have a 3 year old biological son and a foster 3 year old girl that's been full-time with us for 10 months. I'll gloss over the details, but I have never developed any attachment nor have I felt love for the little girl. I have still acted as a dad for her as best as I could, but it has drained me and I've had a burnout. As a result I told my partner that I would stop being responsible for her, and minimize my time around her, until I figure a way to not be so unhappy in her presence. My partner lives with her mother and I live 5 mins away, we've always been both quite independent of each other - so this arrangement is something that works for us currently.

Obviously things could be better. I see my partner and my son less as a result of this arrangement. If I can manage to spend time with this little girl without being mentally exhausted, it's all the better for everyone. I see three ways this could happen:

  1. I somehow become able to tolerate the behavioral issues of this little girl
  2. We find a way to discipline her so she behaves
  3. She begins feeling securely attached

On (1): I don't have any idea of how to proceed. I am able to stay cool in the face of the occasional tantrums from my son. But when it comes from her, I am way more susceptible. She is constantly demanding for attention in whatever way possible and it drives me crazy. Without feeling attached to her, I don't see how I could withstand that on a regular basis. Even if I were to work on some anger management, it wouldn't help with the mental exhaustion. I have been thinking of therapy but I don't see exactly which kind, considering that my reaction is fairly normal.

On (2): I am biased but I think that the way I do it works. I am caring but strict. I will give her affection during bonding time, and never when she asks for it in an excessive or inappropriate manner. After a couple of months together, she has come to behave like a regular child when I am alone with her, and I can tolerate her then. But it only works if it's just the two of us. My partner is not as strict, as her attachment to her is different and as she does not want to feel cruel in difficult times. This little girl knows that and she will regularly push my partner to the extreme so she can get attention. When we're looking from professional advice, we essentially get told to bear with it. That we should tell her that her behavior is inappropriate and that she matters to us without needing her to draw our attention to us. But isolating her as punishment is supposedly a no-no, and that's the only thing I can do not to go insane. We've been following these guidelines for weeks, and I don't see any change happening in her.

On (3): I have tried many things. I read a book on attachment issues. We've been to parent-child bonding activities together. We've seen quite a few professionals. Still, this girl is only preoccupied by whether her foster mom or dad are paying attention to her. We've been told that 10 months living with us is nothing, that it'll take many more years to maybe get there. I am in denial about that. I refuse to believe that there isn't a way a child who has been separated from her parents can chill out with her new family after a couple of months. How ridiculous is the human condition that a child with attachment issues will do precisely the things that put them at risk of not being kept in their foster family? I get that she's testing us but to what point? It's not helping her situation.

A couple of notes:

  • My partner sees this child as her own, and has no plans of sending her away ever.
  • I make no bets in what the future will be. I could get attached to this girl. I could also not be attached, but become able to tolerate her. The current arrangement I have with my partner could last also a long time.
  • There are currently no tensions with the way things are. All four of us are doing ok. Given our way of life, there would be nothing to gain in a proper separation with my partner.

July 2025 edit: Thanks to everyone who replied, I have carefully read your answers and truly appreciate them. I want to add some context:

  • The situation has evolved so that we spend more time together as 4, but it remains that I am not feeling serene, connected, attached to our girl. My "attachment" to her is unfortunately conditional: when she acts like a normal little girl I am happy to have her around, but when all she does is seek out our attention, I just wish she'd be gone. I do my best to treat her equally to my son, with whom I have such an easy time feeling compassion for.
  • I have autism. A lot of you picked up on the fact that I speak rather coldly and bluntly about the situation, and you've hit home. I have this very emotionally detached manner of speaking about my life, but the good news is that it paints a darker image than what actually is. It's difficult to reason about my attachment with our girl and to put myself in her shoes. My autism is definitely a large part of the equation, and it's hard to figure out whether it will be at all possible for me to bond with her, even following the good advice I have been given here and in therapy. But I can't just rule it out on that basis.
  • Becoming a foster parent was initially something I wanted to "try", and despite being warned early on that there was no such thing as trying a child, I played along with my partner who was deeply willing to be a foster parent. It was the second day I visited our little girl that I realized it would be very difficult for me, and my partner was not at all ready to turn back then. We had several arguments and the decision was very difficult to make. I have considered leaving my partner months later, but we love eachother very much, so I stuck around best as I could.

title: What is the science on preteen kids playing moderate (less than 9 h /wk) video games?
body:
What are long term effects of preteen kids playing moderate video games? Or is it the same as any screen time? The axes I'm most interested in are

  • competitive vs cooperative,
  • screen time vs video game time (passive vs active),
  • playing together in-person vs playing alone (regardless of online multiplayer)

I'm clicking through search results on pubmed but I'm not so good at this. I am only interested in projected long term psychosocial effects.

The backstory is that I have a couple kids who are currently not playing games much. I have started playing games with them for cuddle time because when I start to play they come and cuddle with me which is, frankly, good for my mental health. So it's daddy time. Social, not a babysitter, and nonviolent. But it is addictive. They ask me to play the next day, or again the same evening. Honestly I've taken it as an opportunity to teach moderation, and emphasize that we have to be able to stop quickly for any reason. Like a conversation, homework, bedtime, etc. I have repeated (and modeled) this lesson many times. But now my partner is concerned because she sees the signs of addiction too. So what do longitudinal studies on video games say?

There is no chance we aren't going to moderate the time, and while I plan to allow occasional solo play (eg 3D mental rotation is something my daughter can benefit from practicing and I have a couple puzzle games that are good for that), mainly I want to use games to get cuddles while I still can.

One significant factor is that my younger son is autistic and we are therefore appropriately concerned about his long term social development, which is a challenge currently.

title: How can I encourage my toddler to try new foods?
body:
I have a two year old daughter who is generally a very good eater. When she was a bit younger she was always willing to at least take a bite of two of any new food that I would put on her plate, but lately she has started to completely refuse anything outside of her set of favorite foods. Those favorite foods are pretty varied, so it could be worse, but I really want to encourage her to try more things (especially vegetables, where she unsurprisingly the most picky).

I've tried including a food that I know she likes (typically fruit or pasta or meatballs/loaf) on the plate with the new food, but she'll just eat the thing she likes and then throw her plate on the floor with the stuff she doesn't want to try. I understand that part of this is the developmentally normal boundary testing that they do at this age, but I've come up short trying to get her to try new foods that I really think she would enjoy based on the things that she does eat. I'm not super thrilled about the "you eat this or you eat nothing" method that I've had recommended to me, especially since she always seems to choose the latter when we resort to it.

title: Toddler (2 1/2 year old boy) won’t sleep without mum or dad in his bedroom
body:
Wondering if anyone has a solution for a phase we are going through with our 2 1/2 year old son. Since before he was 2, our son has had some real issues with sleeping alone in his room.

He has a pretty typical routine where:

  • Dinner around 6-6.30pm
  • Playtime 7.30-7pm
  • Bath time 7-7.30pm
  • 7.30-8pm PJs on and read a book.
  • 8-8.30pm Milk in cot to fall asleep.

The problem we are facing is that as soon we finish the book, he immediately asks for one of us to sit next to his bed or on the double bed we have in his room as he knows we are about to put him into his cot for bed time. You can actively see the anxiety on his face and hear it in his voice as soon as he knows he has to sleep and that we might leave.

The only way we can get him to sleep now is by lying in the bed in his room till he falls asleep, we then leave to go into our bedroom.

He’ll then wake up at midnight crying out and we’ll have to go in and stroke his head (we normally wait in case he falls back to sleep but he never does) until he falls asleep and then leave to go back to our bedroom.

The next wake up will be 3am and he then cries out even louder and this wake up he needs us to stay in the room with him otherwise he won’t go back to sleep. Both these wake ups are like clockwork and require the same method to get him back to sleep.

We’ve tried all the methods:

  • I’ll be right back - extending the returns more and more. This resulted in him becoming more worked up each time it got longer and longer.

  • Cry it out - walk out after saying good night and cuddles etc. we left him for over an hour crying and calling out, jumping in his cot, till we finally went in to comfort him. This was an awful experience for all of us and I don’t know if we could stomach that again.

  • Edging closer to the door each night. Similar to the "I’ll be right back" approach, he just got more anxious each time we got closer to the door.

  • Sleeping on the floor/bed and moving that closer to door. Same result as when we sat on the floor moving closer to the door, he would just get more anxious the closer we got.

If anyone has gone through this before, it would be great to hear how you dealt with this. Even to hear that you ended up just staying in their room and the phase passed, I think hearing how long it took would give us some peace knowing there is light at the end of the tunnel and knowing how long that realistically could be.

Thank you community!

Dad

title: Child accuses friend of stealing
body:

Realistically, anyone could have stolen it. If he accuses his friend it will hurt his friends feelings. While this is something we will talk about, I'm not sure we should talk about it some more and then leave it to him to decide what to do. In this case i plan to tell him to discuss the disappeared money with his class or at least with a group of friends without accusing anyone in particular. Is this the right course of action?

On one hand it feels wrong to disregard his hunch and to tell him to keep his suspicions to himself, even when it will bother him a lot. On the other hand, he has no proof and an accusation like this could ruin their friendship. They are only 11.

title: Daughter might be showing signs of ASD?
body:
I have a lovely DD who today just turned 21 months and I am pretty sure she has some ASD traits.

Positive

  1. She can say up to 100 words.
  2. She can do pointing, waves and claps, and pretend playing.
  3. She has always brought us toys / books etc, follow commands to an extent like "it's bath time."
  4. She is also a good sleeper, she can self settle after the bottle.
  5. She imitates everything.
  6. She has good joint attention and always look where I am pointing.
  7. She can put two words together.
  8. She is very engaging and saying hello and smiling to people who engage with her.
  9. She can identify animals on books and tv correctly .
  10. She understands simple commands like "Time to go out," "bath time," "get your shoes," "shut the door," "pick it up," or "get me baby dolly"
  11. She can tell me when she does a "poo"
  12. She can answer the questions "What’s that?" and "Where is dolly?"
  13. She is very affectionate.

Reason to worry:

  1. She tenses up and tippy toes when excited since she was 14 months.

  2. She rotates her wrists and ankles when excited, always done. It’s what worries me most.

  3. Occasionally she does side glancing when turning her head to look at something behind her shoulders.

  4. She doesn’t answer simple questions like "Do you want milk?"

  5. She has an extraordinary memory.

My HV (health visitor, a nurse who comes to check up on the child), and doctor don’t see a reason to assess her. Now I understand that would be close to impossible getting a diagnosis or assessment based on this but was wondering if any of your kids had this presentation . Many thanks ☺️

title: How to deal with an older toddler who refuses to eat anything but cheerios?
body:
Our three year old is developing another bad habit - he absolutely refuses to eat anything except bowl after bowl of cheerios!

...Well okay it's not that bad - he will sometimes try new foods he is curious about, and he will gladly scarf down yogurt pouches and usually goes for nutrigrain bars too.

But he gets extremely upset if we don't constantly keep a little bowl of cheerios at the ready for him - tugging on our finger to beg us for them (he is speech delayed) and even throwing a fit if we refuse to give him any (and refusing to eat anything else).

He is, for the most part, doing okay on his nutrition, but he used to eat a much more varied number of foods, and I'm worried about him developing a bad habit of only ever filling up on cheerios.

What should we do?

title: Stressed out highschooler
body:
I have an amazing son; he is a very good person, likes helping people, patient, sweet and very hard working. However, he doesn't know when to stop trying and ask for help. He is enrolled in a highly competitive STEM-magnet program in high school and he is usually stressed out.

With lots of school work, projects, and college prep etc., he can't go to bed early, and when he tries to go to bed, it takes him a lot of time to fall asleep. And then he is tired the next day.

Obviously, it has become a cycle and weekends aren't helping either as he needs to catch up on long-term projects/clubs from school. As a parent, I feel helpless in this situation, and have nothing to do other than encourage him that he is doing well. How are other teenagers handling this stress, their time and all the workload?

title: How to deal with difficult parents who takes things for granted and won't take accountability for student's lack of discipline?
body:
By profession, I am a young computer engineer who has agreed to provide tutoring for computer science and AI to a girl studying in higher secondary school in India. She is from a family in the neighborhood, whose parents are somewhat good neighborhood friends of my parents. I gave her a strict day and time for her tutoring sessions which is Friday at 7 PM. However, she tends to skip the sessions occasionally, or she delays joining the sessions, attending very late. Over that, her parents expect me to be available any time to teach her because they reside very near to me and they expect that their daughter can come anytime to me and I will teach her, or make up for her missed sessions, etc.

When it comes to her other sessions, if she has another tutoring session with someone else that conflicts with my day and time (which is again on Friday at 7 PM), then her parents allow her to skip my classes and join that other tutoring session instead. After my session is skipped, her parents also expect that I make up for the session that she misses and manage to get me to agree by speaking in a way that's very clever and persuades me to allow it.

Yesterday, I talked with her father (who is the main person who takes my time, efforts and availability for granted). I clearly and boldly told him that I won't tolerate the lack of discipline and punctuality of his daughter's attendance, and I won't be making up for the sessions that she misses from her end. I also requested him not to take my classes for granted and give equal importance to my tutoring sessions, just like they give for the other tutors.

Furthermore, I told him that any additional skipping of tutoring sessions and I won't be able to make up for her because the burden keeps increasing. The multiple delays means that all the chapters that were supposed to be finished on time are now being pushed later and they will pile up and cause huge burden just before the final exams.

But her father instead started to get defensive about his daughter. He also started to question me on why I did not inform about his daughter's lack of discipline and punctuality before. I was stunned. Being her father, doesn't he know that his daughter is not being disciplined and punctual in attending my tutoring sessions? Is it not his responsibility as her parent? In fact, he is the one who gave her the freedom and flexibility to come to my tutoring sessions at any time she wants because she resides nearby, ruining all her discipline and sense of commitment to attend the sessions sincerely and study.

I somehow think that my efforts, time and availability are taken for granted. I am thinking that her father and mother think that I will do anything that they say and adapt according to their requests. And when I am approaching her parents regarding the lack of discipline and punctuality of their daughter, then her parents are going on the defensive instead of trying to come up with a solution.

How do I make the parents understand this situation without being too bold or rude?

title: Should I worry because my toddler prefers sleeping on the floor?
body:
My 2,5 year old toddler decided she wants to sleep in her own room a week ago. She has a loft bed, the lower part of which is clad in wood as a castle with a mattress in it. The upper part is locked with a door so that she cannot climb up when she is alone in the room. For several nights now, I have noticed that she is moving further and further away from her bed at night. Sometimes she lies on the threshold between the bed and the floor, sometimes she lies completely on the floor in her room. I have already placed an exercise mat in front of her bed, but she also crawls off it at night.

The floor of her room is covered with laminate and a thin carpet and seems terribly hard and uncomfortable to me, so I wonder if this is an issue worth worrying about. She seems content and wants to go back to her room every night. I'm not worried about her hurting herself as the nursery is child safe. Is this just an oddity of children or should I take action? If so, does it make sense to make it harder for her to get out of bed or does it restrict her too much? She doesn't crawl out of the normal height parents bed when she sleeps there (as she has for the last 2,5 years).

title: 10 year old dealing with ADHD or Autism-like symptoms and introducing management techniques
body:
I need to lead this with the fact that there is no official diagnosis yet - this is merely initial comparisons made by school counsellors.

So it has been suggested that my 10 year old son is dealing with a lack of awareness regarding:

  • understanding his emotions, and emotional expression - he gets visibly frustrated/angry at things, but claims he is "fine".
  • recognising certain behaviours; he claims he is being bullied "by everyone" for being "weird", when he has a rather intense energy, especially when his emotions are heightened; has very little to no spacial awareness, often getting very close to others; and acting like a "puppy" with any one he looks up to/treats him nicely (getting close, assuming a happy "begging" stance). This is more common with strangers or acquaintances, rather than close friends or relatives, and primarily adults (perhaps figures of authority?).
  • recognising his own contributions to conflicts. For example, he may be frustrated at something, and an unrelated input may frustrate him further, causing him to lash out, and causing a conflict. When the person affected retaliates, that's when there is a problem - he "did nothing", and they acted out towards him for "no reason".
  • He prefers natural light, (preferring darker light levels) over artificial light, and can get easily overstimulated with light levels, noise and cramped conditions
  • Constant pacing when unoccupied, unless interrupted. He again sees nothing wrong with this behaviour, even though this consistently leads to frustration of having nothing to do, and not wanting to do anything, aside from constant screen time (Minecraft or Mario Kart, YouTube, iPad games, etc).
  • Impulse control is a big one - constantly stealing snacks and drinks, or to play games or on his iPad, and makes efforts to wake up early (setting his alarm for 5.30) in order to attempt this, or actively hides his actions (usually by hiding the evidence in his room).
  • When he has trouble sleeping, he simply turns lights on, regardless of how many times he is told not to do this, and ask for music or grey/white noise (rain sounds or running water) instead, which to relax him and keep him calm, rather than keep him more awake.
  • Constant asking for the same things, only remembering when he has been told "later", and never when he has been told "no".

Efforts we have made to help or control this (as well as suggestions we have been given):

  • fidget toys, and to encourage their use when calm, to help create a sense of calming for when he is agitated
  • physical activity, like running around, kicking a ball, jumping on the trampoline, which he often refuses. He is currently enrolled in a martial arts class once a week, which he very much enjoys, but when it's suggested he practice his "set" at home, he refuses as well.
  • reading to help calm before bed (has only recently been getting into one book, which has been difficult in the past), but he only does this when he wants to, when he is not in the "bored" mindset.
  • limiting screen time; we do currently limit screen time to 1 hour, regardless of type and end all screen time half an hour before bed, but allow more over the weekend, extending it to a few hours depending on what is happening.
  • talking him through conflicts and helping him become aware of his own actions, emotions and expressions, however this often causes him to become more upset, leading him to blame and put himself down.

These are only new adjustments, so the resistances and responses are understandable, and we have been told that he will struggle with these behaviours throughout his teenage years. We do have another 12 year old who is beginning to enter his teenage phase, already reaching puberty, dealing with peer pressures, his own obsessions and resistance to rules and restrictions, etc., making this new adjustment particularly straining on us as parents.

Are there any tactics we can employ to help adopt these techniques?

Additionally, I want to introduce him to the concept of his antics. As an example, I have Epilepsy, and before this diagnosis when I was 25 (roughly 10 years ago), I was unable to understand what was going on - a lack of focus, or an inability to comprehend conversation at times; getting "dizzy spells" and nausea, and lapses in memory. Once I received this diagnosis, these symptoms made sense, making it less frustrating and easier to manage and adjust.

Introducing him to his (potential) condition may help his understanding, but I am hesitant because this diagnosis is not official (we are waiting on an appointment with a Paediatrician), and the potential of identifying as "Autistic". Again, as an example, I see my self as "myself; with Epilepsy" - this is not who I am as a person, this is just an aspect of my physiology, in the same way that I am shortsighted - I simply need to manage this; as opposed to "being an Epileptic", and defining my life through these restrictions.

I want to ask if I should do this, though that will potentially draw opinions - I am uncertain. But if I do, how should I go about this with a young, impressionable mind?

title: Baby fake eating
body:
So I have a 3 week old, born 7 days before term, 3.5kg on birth, lost almost 400g in the hospital, then returned to 3.5kg in about 10 days. Since then he has gained an additional 200g, which I fear is not enough.

title: How much should I make ADHD 8 year old work to solve puzzles before I give hints?
body:
My 8 year old, soon to be 9, niece loves lateral thinking puzzles and has been asking me for them regularly. For context these are puzzles where you are given a strange situation and have to figure out what is happening with only yes or no questions. They usually involve at least one 'lateral leap', ie realizing something unintuitive or an intentional trick hidden within the puzzle to solve them as well.

She's liked them ever since she solved her first one years ago - she got lots of hints but considering how young she was then it was pretty impressive she solved it at all so I praised her for it. Just yesterday she was practically shouting in glee that the kid in my puzzle was blind when she finally figured out why the child 'never saw his father again'; but she only got there once I started getting pretty helpful and volunteering extra details I'm not suppose to give to her questions designed to get her to realize her presumption that something bad happened to the father couldn't be right.

She is pretty good at solving the 'lateral leap', for her age at least. Her biggest problem is that she wants to leap straight to guessing the answer. while more complicated puzzles usually require starting with more general questions designed to narrow down the situation and get more detail before one knows enough to have a realistic chance of solving the puzzle. I've been trying to tell her this and encourage her to start asking more of these generalized questions rather then trying to jump to the solution, with limited success.

Right now my biggest problem is she gets frustrated and starts asking for hints quickly. If she can't solve it all in one go she wants a hint to point her in the right direction rather then working towards methodically asking questions to expand her understanding of the situation. I like how the puzzles engage her problem solving skills, but feel she would get more out of them if I pushed her to work more to try and solve her confusion herself before she get's hints; but I don't want to make the puzzles so frustrating for her that she stops wanting to do them.

I also have the problem that I can't provide puzzles fast enough to satisfy her. I'd dare say I'm pretty decent at coming up with these sorts of puzzles, but she goes through them so quickly, thanks partially to all the hints she demands, that I just can't come up with puzzles fast enough to keep up with her demands and I'm starting to struggle with finding new puzzles she hasn't heard yet online to supplement the ones I create at this point. If we don't slow her down somehow I'm going to reach a point where I simply have no puzzles to offer her soon.

My biggest problem is that when I delay hints she starts begging for them more and more or just declare she gives up and want's the answer rather then continuing to try to solve the puzzle. I've tried to explain the steps to get better at solving the puzzles, even giving 'hints' that were basically to ask more questions about a specific subject since that would lead to more information. But my niece still tends to demand instant gratification and doesn't seem to want to try if she can't guess the answer all at once.

I should probably mention she is ADHD and by the time we get to puzzles her medication has usually worn off and she's hyperactive, which no doubt contributes to her inpatients.

So how much work should she have to put in to before she get's help, and how do I keep her engaged and interested when I delay giving her hints?

title: Regressions in potty-training
body:
This summer we went through potty-training with our daughter (26 months at the time). I had the feeling it was still a bit early for her (she wasn't showing much interest) but decided to do it anyway because it was a moment where I could be close to her and give her a lot of care and attention. She picked up easily enough and in 3-4 weeks she was diaperless. We used to take her out, at the park, in the car for longish trips without issue. She was staying dry during afternoon naps and most nights too.

Then in September she went back to daycare (she went last year too and never had any issues there) and she had a massive regression. We were expecting a bit of going backwards but it's been massive, she would not hold anything at all and wet herself even every 1/2h. Together with the daycare staff we tried to hold the line and not going back to diapers when she's awake (we had to put the nappies back for the afternoon and night) but in the end it was untenable and back to diapers she went. I still tried to keep her without at home in the afternoon because I felt badly for her to let her lose a competence that way.

However, a couple of weeks ago I kept her at home for a few days because she had a bad cold and by the end of the week she was back to the level she was at this summer. She would hold the pee for much longer, tell me if she needed to poo or pee and when I took her she would be dry/clean and go in the toilet. In short it seemed like it had "clicked" with her and she was toilet trained again and out of the regression. Then she went back to daycare and, in 4 days time, she was regressing again as badly as before. She regularly poos in her pants every day and wets herself multiple times in a few hours span.

I am at my wits end and I don't know what to do. The daycare seems clearly to be the problem, but she does not show any obvious issue there. She seems to go happily enough, she doesn't cry and when we go and fetch her she is playing happily with the other kids. More context: she is our second child, she is a very good-natured girl, she was always calm, kind and well-adapted (unlike her older brother) even though now she is entering the terrible twos and it shows in many respects.

Has anybody gone through something similar? Do you have any suggestions?

Or when we go outside meet our friends, when we have to communicate to each other in English as well? I know that my baby will learn English eventually when she goes to the nursery or primary school. title: How do chores fit in with positive discipline?
body:
My boys are still young (2.75 and 4.5), and they do a lot of natural helping, so I'm not entirely sure if they're ready for firm, consistent responsibilities yet, but I'm interested to know how best to make this work with positive discipline, and what age is appropriate to get chores started.

At the moment we don't force them to do any particular thing unless they've made a mess in an obvious, anti-social way. Occasionally they'll help us clean up, occasionally they say no and we clean up, for the most part we don't make a big deal about it unless it's a behavior that needs correcting.

So with positive discipline I'm interested in understanding what the most appropriate way is to make this non-dramatic approach work when they're older and they refuse to do some of their chores. My wife and I are both agreed that we don't want to tie their chores to an allowance, because cleaning and organizing is just a part of life that they need to learn.

But that leads to the question of: what exactly do we do in response to the situation where they aren't doing their chores or fulfilling some of their responsibilities? We don't want to punish them in a hurtful way, or force them, but we do want to teach them personal responsibility. So what would be an appropriate way to encourage fulfilling their responsibilities without negative reinforcement?

title: Consistency between parents around bedtime routine
body:
We have a 10mo who sleeps solidly 11h at night. Almost always cries when going to bed but usually asleep within 5-10min. Quite a happy kid so we reckon the cry is just tired or FOMO. We have a routine, put into cot awake, bum pat and say goodnight.

Dad sits in a chair in the dark in the far end of room (and she can see him a bit I reckon) and is on his phone, she falls asleep. I disappear into the walk in robe where she can’t see me, she falls asleep. If she can’t fall asleep herself and cries out after 3-4min we bum pat her and say goodnight phrase again. We haven’t needed to do extra pats too often.

  1. do dad and I need to do the same thing after pats and goodnight ie either the chair or the wardrobe to maintain consistency? Or does it not matter as long as we go to her in the same reassuring way and do the same pats if she needs it?

  2. I would like to be able to work on us leaving the room eventually but dad is hesitant as this change has cause the settle to take a longer time and he’s not ready, and he thinks she’s not ready either. How did you know when your baby was ‘ready’ for this transition?

title: Authorative opinion on swaddling
body:
In the past when a decision on parenting was needed, I usually looked for an authorative source. For example by following the Dutch Health Service we decided to give 1 shot, but not another.

However, despite searching I have not found an authorative source with a recommendation on whether to swaddle.

I am not looking for opinions, or explanations on pros/cons or context of how often it is being done. I am also not looking fot information on how (not) to do it. I am simply looking for guidance from an authorative source. It could be a yes/no or a basic decision tree.

Ideally the source would be a country or regional organization (e.g. WHO,NHS,...) responsible for health advice. A research is always done with a specific scope, so university recommendations would come in at a lower point for me.

Best would be from The Netherlands, but if not that is fine.

If there are multiple conflicting guidelines from the most relevant authorities that would be good to know as well.

title: Can one appeal to helpfulness when asking a tween to do chores?

title: 5 year Old son is extremely stressed
body:
My son is very stressed about various things.

He is afraid to do activities with children he doesn't know, and even though he would like to participate, he stays in his corner and plays alone. He is in kindergarten (final year) and is already scared of the end-of-year school celebration. He wasn't able to join the end-of-year dance in middle and lower kindergarten because he was too anxious and cried too much. This happens from time to time to one kid out of 20 in a class in lower kindergarten, but for him it's gonna be the third year in a row.

He always needs to know that his parents, or perhaps more specifically, his father, are nearby. He doesn’t want to sleep alone and cries at the mere thought that we might not be the first ones to pick him up from school.

We have a lot of ideas about where all this might come from. I (the father) also used to be an introvert when I was young, although quite far from what my son is experiencing now. My wife went abroad with our son and newborn for a few months in the beginning of last year. Our son didn't enjoy the separation. I have to travel every two months or so for a few days. We now also spend time with our baby, so we have less time for him than before. Although, I almost feel that I spend more time with my son than with my one year old toddler.

We have tried a lot of things to help him. Talking to him about his feelings and try to put words on his fears. Reassure him that we are never going to leave him alone. We tried various baby steps to get him to get better. For example simply "Say hi to people we meet". We also try to congratulate him on all his little successes.

This year, he is joining activities with other kids, and after 5 trainings of this activity, I made it to leave the room for a few minutes. One thing to add, is that he wanted to join these activities from the start. One of them he seemingly is really good at, so he is also with almost only older kids.

I feel that there are a few improvements but on some sides he almost gets worse. The crying at the thought that we're not coming first to pick him up started last week after my mother-in-law came 5 minutes late to the school. (I also arrived 10 minutes late last month following a misunderstanding with my wife).

We are going to take appointments with a teacher and maybe with a psychiatrist, as we are not sure how to help anymore. If anyone has other ideas/insights we would be grateful!

title: My 16 year old niece is punching her mother (my sister)
body:
My sister (50 yrs old) had been married to a man who verbally and emotionally abused her for 15 years. He presents as having narcissistic personality disorder. She finally divorced him 1 year ago after a verbal threat to shoot her that was heard by others and an order of protection was established for my sister and her house. The children (15 &11 at the time) were not included in this.

Since then, my older niece has become more aggressive, verbally,towards my sister until things came to a head around Halloween when she punched her mother repeatedly in the face while yelling "This is your fault! You are making me do this!" (The outburst happened when my sister was asking her what time her friends were coming to get her and the teen ignored her and tried slamming the door in her face.) She left the home to live with her father. For some further background, my ex brother in law was not a bad father to his girls and my sister has been able to co-parent with him decently since he moved out, but he DID frequently blame her for any of his misfortune.

I feel very strongly that my sister has been through enough of this that she should consider letting her ex raise the teenager solely on his own. My sister has tried to get her outside counselling (she refused to get out of the car) and she has gone through the high school counsellor as well (my niece refused to speak). At this point my sister is going to the therapist she set up for her daughter to learn ways around the teen's brick wall and nothing has worked. My younger niece (who has also been a frequent punching bag for her older sibling) recently came home from her time at her dad's house and told my sister that the teen won't come home because that would mean her mom "won".

I work with children and I have seen a litany of behaviors that can usually be addressed if you can get to the root of the problem. The aggression doesn't concern me so much (although I am not thrilled about that), but what she yelled at her mother while she was hitting/biting her, "This is your fault! You are making me do this!" This seems abnormal.

Everything in me wants my niece to go far away from my sister, but that's my emotional mind, not my rational mind speaking. How should my sister proceed if they can't even agree that violence isn't the answer? She's trying everything she knows how to do to get help for a teen that refuses it. Are there other avenues or resources outside of therapy that could help? Are there mediators for situations like this?

title: Tracking Medicines
body:
When our kids are sick and need meds it can be pretty overwhelming keeping track of when each kid last got each dose of what meds, and when they can get a “next dose.” This is especially true when the kids are sick (high stress) in the middle of the night (when we're exhausted), and often when we're also managing other symptoms (vomit in particular comes to mind).

Currently my wife and I have settled into sending each other an SMS text message like this:

Tiger, Cough Syrup 1 Tbsp, 2:50pm
Bugaboo, Vomited, 1:41am; temperature 100.1
Bugaboo, Acetaminophen 2 tablets, 2:16am; fever 102.5
Tiger, Cough Syrup 1 Tbsp, 3:01am
Bugaboo, Ibuprofen 1 tablet, 4:16am; fever 101.9

please note these numbers are completely invented

This is ok but it requires searching back for the most recent dose, doing simple math when we're sleep deprived, and it risks missing a text and dosing too often, or not often enough.

We’ve historically used:

  • A whiteboard (inconvenient, in the kitchen, not our bedroom)
  • Timers on our phones (only on one of our phones, not shared)
  • Sticky notes on each bottle (we have multiple bottles of several medicines)
  • shared google keep or Apple note (easier than SMS since it's dedicated, but less convenient to find)
  • None of these make it easy to see at a glance how long ago each kid got each dose of each med.

They all work, but there’s got to be something better out there. What do you use to keep track of when you last gave a sick kid medicine, especially with a partner?
