title: Raising a tri-lingual child - alternate by days
body:
My wife and I speak languages A, B, and C.

I am native at A and my wife is native at B.

We are both highly proficient at C.

We live in a B-speaking country.

We want our upcoming child to be fluent at all three languages.

Our plan is to alternate through the three languages on a daily basis.

Meaning: today we speak A, tomorrow B, the day after - C, and so on.

We intend to try to have as full immersion in each day's language as possible: read, watch TV, listen to music, etc. - in the day's language (as well as speak to each other in the day's language in front of the child).

From what I've read, OPOL (one parent - one language) seems to be a more common strategy.

I am interested in hearing opinions and experiences with our planned approach.

title: Why do grown-ups not taking kiddos seriously?
body:
Why is there an automatic assumption that any child would lose automatically?

When your child wants to race you at the playground on the kiddie rock wall, why is there this assumption that your child can’t actually race you? Children can climb a rock wall, why else are these on the playground? Instead it seems that grown-ups will just barely move, and act like the Kiddie  wall is the hardest thing ever. Why not actually climb, and actually race your child like they are wanting you to do? The whole point of a rock wall races to see who can get to the top first.

It is the same thing when a child wants to arm wrestle with them the adult seemingly barely even does much of anything, and it is very obvious that they are just straight up letting their kid win. Why doesn’t the adult actually put in effort when they arm wrestle? Why not actually challenge your kid, the whole point of arm wrestling is to see who is stronger. If the opponent loses then they just need to provide a little bit more strength. Why is there this automatic assumption that any child would lose or not be able to play with them?

I have also noticed this when parents have a running relay race with their child. Why don’t the parents actually run? Instead they will sort of do this really awkward walking, and they end up just letting their kid win. The whole point of a running race is to see Who is going to get there first. Why not actually run and actually challenge your kid? Your child just needs to run a little bit faster next time to actually be able to win. Again, there seems to be this automatic assumption that a child can’t run, they have running tracks on the playground as well, so children can run.

If you were to play with a friend it’s not any different. Why would you automatically assume that your friend can’t play? If you’re going to arm wrestle with your friend, do it with your kid, if you’re going to run when you race your friend, do that with your kid . Same thing with Rockwall climbing on the playground with your child. Actually climb, just like you would do with your friend. Why isn’t that just because it’s a child wanting to arm wrestle or climb on the rock wall etc., most adults just come to the conclusion that they are going to lose and can’t play just because they’re a kid in elementary school?

title: Car seat Advice?
body:
I wanted to get your opinion on if we should keep her current car seat or get something different. Right now my 6YO daughter Clara has Primordial dwarfism which puts her at 1’5” tall and 18 pounds Right now we have her in a rear facing infant bucket car seat, she has plenty of room to grow into it as she has the newborn insert installed with plenty of room currently, and given how she is growing, we are not sure when she will outgrow her current car seat, she will most likely be able to use this car seat for years and years . I feel as though this is the only car seat that is safe for her. Given how fragile she is physically (similar to an infant if not more) mixed in with her height and weight. In terms of height she is smaller than a newborn, and in terms of physical development it is comparable to an 8 month old depending on what you were looking at. We have also been told to keep her on a newborn recline because of this. She uses the newborn insert because of her muscle and bone development and how fragile she is, and five point Because this is a rear facing infant bucket, it doubles as an infant carrier. This is extremely useful given that Clara tires out very easily due to her size and strength. Should we keep using the bucket seat or not?

is there also a way she could be able to climb up into it herself? Right now I usually lift her into the car seat, I am buckling her in just like anyone would with it your typical infant, due to her physical limitations. Anything can be half her height or more. It would be amazing if Clara could climb all the way from the ground up into her car seat and buckle herself in completely on her own. Given her height, the regular seat is pretty high up for her, and any car seat makes it quite a bit higher for her than it already is, even more so a rear facing. It would still be awesome if she could climb up herself safely because she doesn’t want to be treated like a toddler and lift it up into the car seat, we would also need something to help her climb up onto the floorboard, and then from there up onto the seat. Right now she isn’t tall enough to climb up on the floorboard, and even if she did she again isn’t tall enough to climb up onto the regular car chair. She also has trouble climbing over the side to get into her car seat seat. Even when it is on the ground the sides are slightly too tall for her to climb in. Does anyone have any ideas on how Clara can climb all the way up to her car seat when it is installed?

title: Highchair advice?
body:
Our daughter has a dwarfism and is 1’5” tall and 18 pounds. We are looking for something to know raise her all the way up to the table while also giving her the independence and ability to climb in and out of her chair by herself. She really needs a highchair to be up at the right height, but given that she is six years old we are trying to find something a little more age-appropriate that also gets her up high enough. Does anyone have any experience with the Tripp Teapp Hi dear would it be small enough for her to fit into, while also Raising her up high enough? We also need to keep in mind the steps up into the chair, and making sure that they are close enough together that she can reach them.

What should we do about this when we go to restaurants?. I would love to get her all the way up to be able to eat comfortably and be a part of the conversation, not just under the table. We would need to find something for both chairs and booths that could be adjustable given that at each different location the height are really different and not really known. We have tried the boosters that they provide and that usually only brings her high enough for us to only see the very top of her hair, or for her to be able to barely see over the table when she stretches up as high as she can, and in booth she still isn’t close enough.

The ideal highchair that we are looking for at home would be one that is able to slide under the table a little while also having a seat high enough so Clara can sit right up at the table and rest her feet in the highchair and eat from her plate. We can help her with everything else that is too far for her to reach, but at least she would be able to reach her plate nice and comfortable. also if there was a latter for her to climb up by herself. We could modify the existing ladder on the backside and switch out the handles for much smaller ones and even add a couple lower so she can be able to reach them. Unlike a traditional baby/toddlers highchair which only brings them up high to the table but they are still sitting pretty far back because they are being helped with feeding and other things. What would you recommend here??

title: What are age appropriate consequences for an 11 year old "light" stealing/taking without asking?
body:
We have an 11 year old who is generally well behaved for an 11 year old.

We try to teach natural consequences for things (e.g. you left the games on the floor and so now I've taken them and you have to do something special to get them back)

Recently he took my partners (his mother/other parent) Nintendo Switch (so he could use the controllers) without permission. It's not the first time he's snuck digital toys -- usually when he's caught, the consequence is that his screen time is revoked for a period of time (along with a discussion of why what he did was wrong).

Are there any other age-appropriate consequences that we can provide? In particular something to help him understand that he violated the property rights and trust of his mother, and how he can commit restitution?

title: Taking my daughter to the zoo?
body:
We were thinking of taking a family trip to the zoo. Our 6 YO daughter is 1‘5“ tall and 18 pounds due to dwarfism. typically when we are out with her, we carry her around in her car seat when she isn’t walking with us. I was wondering if anyone had any suggestions for when we are at the zoo with her?

Typically when you’re at the zoo you are looking all around, so I wanted to ask what others thought would be better given this. We could bring her car seat, which does have a stroller attachment. We also have a traditional stroller that she can sit in, and we also do have a baby carrier that we can wear. We don’t typically use the baby carrier just because of her age, but this would bring her up a lot higher so she will be able to see over the fences. She would be in sort of swaddled so to speak, in the baby carrier facing us, while I’m supporting. right around our chest level.

I just worry if she is in the stroller or in her car seat that she won’t be able to see above any of the fences. Even in the baby carrier I’m not sure if that would be very easy for her to be moving around in looking left and right etc.

Again typically we carry her in the car seat, with her walking around a little bit when she has the energy and isn’t very crowded. But given that we are at the zoo and she needs to be up a lot higher and also able to move around to look in all different directions what would y’all recommend?

title: Potty training ideas for a strong-willed 5 year old
body:
I'll preface this question with the fact that our son, in practice, is potty-trained. He consistently poops on the toilet, and can go full days without an accident. All things considered he fully knows how to use the toilet, and will occasionally take himself to pee when he feels like it, or when someone prompts him.

What makes this question interesting is that our son falls into the category of 'gifted, strong-willed, doesn't care that much'. In other words, he's just not that interested in making it to the toilet 100% of the time, and is happy to soil himself when he's watching TV, or when he's immersed in some fun activity. This is a common theme for similar, strong-willed children.

At this point I figure he just has to mature and eventually make the decision to go consistently himself. But I'm curious if anyone has ever had any type of success in a similar situation, and if there is anything we can actually do. I've resigned myself to being neutral, and trying not to prompt him too much (annoying him). But it seems like no matter what we do the kid is happy to keep peeing on the couch.

ETA: Adding another detail that I figure is relevant. Mom has been overreactive on and off for the past three years, and I believe that has impacted our son's trajectory (he's been discouraged too often). That being said, I'm hesitant to use an overly punitive approach like taking away TV, but I think using a washable chair is a fantastic idea. I may add my own answer later.

title: Wife undermines and interferes in husband's parenting. What role should I play?

title: 6yo has difficulties dealing with others - how to help?
body:
My son is 6 and has a hard time dealing with other kids his age, even his friends. He gets along pretty well with every kid as long as it's only one other one. But as soon as there are two or more, it seems the situation somehow ends up with him there being some sort of "game" which involves all others vs. him, calling names, taking away his stuff, etc. This happens in kindergarten and even when meeting with multiple friends.

As a result, he gets upset and aggressive - throwing things, "getting armed" with sticks, and as a result he is always the one who gets in trouble. He actually isn't very violent, not in general and not even in these situation.

To be clear, I think that focusing on the aggression misses the real point. E.g., aggressive responses are a common pattern when kids are being bullied (not that it is that bad with his friends, but it does sound like what is happening in kindergarten): the victims either withdraw completely, or become aggressive and thus get punished (which further encourages everyone else). Emotional control is obvious a big issue, but I wonder more about why it seems that he always ends up in this situation in the first place.

What can I do to support him? How can we practice better reactions to things that upset him, preparing him for a world where sometimes other kids are mean but that does not mean the end of the world?

title: Spoon-feeding kids before grade school: Do, or Don't?
body:
My partner often spoon feeds our kids before school. One is in kindergarten, the other, 2nd grade. Mostly the younger one, but neither one is very good at eating.

I believe we should put food in front of them, ask them what it's like to be hungry in class, and let them choose to eat, or not. I think the kids would learn to eat if we let them get hungry, and that they have, instead, learned that the food will hover in front of their face if they don't eat it themselves. My partner believes the food needs to get in their stomach for them to be prepared for class, and that this is our responsibility. She will not accept letting the kids be hungry as a learning experience. I think it would be nice if someone spoon-fed me, but I digress.

I am often the one getting the kids ready for school in the morning, and I will spoon feed them a bite or two to help get their appetite started, but my refusal to do more than that is met with scorn when she asks for the report.

Edit:
A previous similar question has a highly rated answer stating that "pressuring children to eat is not only unnecessary, but actively harmful," but, due to the importance of breakfast (I need not be convinced), it seems the argument remains to get the food in the kids' stomach at any cost.

I want my kids to learn to eat, not so that I don't have to feed them, but so that they may feed themselves. Spoon-feeding is less possible as they grow older and more independent, and it seems like my kids still do not know how to eat. My question is not how important is breakfast, but is grade school or primary school breakfast more important than high school and college breakfast?

title: What are good strategies to reduce screen time for an 11-year-old?
body:
My 11-year-old has started spending a significant amount of time on screens lately—mainly watching YouTube, playing online games, and messaging friends. While I understand that some screen time is fine and even educational, I’m worried that it's starting to interfere with other important activities like reading, physical play, and face-to-face family interaction.

I've tried setting limits and encouraging alternative activities, but the pushback is strong—often resulting in arguments or sneaky behavior like hiding devices. I don't want to make it a constant battle, but I also don’t want this to become an unhealthy habit.

Have any particular routines, incentives, or tools worked well for other parents? title: When to introduce my kids to a personal computer?
body:
My wife and I still haven't let our 5 year old do much with our desktop PC, nor any other computing devices, but we do plan on letting our boys use our PC eventually.

Most recommendations I've seen have mentioned that it only makes sense to introduce a PC once they can read, around 6 or 7, and that the main variable involved after that point is controlling their daily screen time.

My question is: is there any type of advantage to introducing them to a PC as early as they can reasonably engage with one? My inclination is to put it off as long as I can and have them focus on real world skills, but I'm wondering if getting their hands on a keyboard can work to our advantage in any way.

This is all with the caveat that their use of the PC would be tightly controlled, guided, and done in a public spot in our home.

title: Our 4 year old hits himself when he's nervous
body:
When our 4 year-old is nervous he will often respond by hitting his head and fake-laughing, grinning or making silly faces while looking to us for a response.

Things that often make him nervous are if he is expected to apologise or say hello/goodbye, or if we're going to meet someone for the first time. He is quite shy generally.

Things we've tried:

  • When he started doing this about a year ago we initially tried gently telling him to not hurt himself, but found that was unproductive. At that stage we had no idea why he was doing it. In retrospect giving him a "no" instruction when he is already exhibiting a stress response was always going to be counterproductive.
  • When we started to realise that anxiety might be the trigger we tried hugging him whenever he did it. Big mistake. That just made him keep going. So at that point we concluded he was seeking attention by doing it.
  • We tried ignoring it completely. This helped. The frequency reduced but hasn't gone away. This is a rather unsatisfying outcome since he's obviously in discomfort when he does it, so it doesn't feel like it addresses the core issue.

We recently visited my uncle for the first time overseas, and as I mentioned to him that we were going to see him tomorrow, he started hitting himself. I thought I'd try something different, and told him that I'm very nervous because I haven't seen my uncle in a long time, and that I'll need lots of hugs to feel better. His face kind of lit up in surprise, he said sometimes like "no, you don't get nervous!" and then gave me a big hug. No hitting.

So I think we've slowly honed in on what this is, ie. He's anxious and he's not able to articulate it or seek comfort in a constructive way.

So while I think we can address the hitting, I don't feel we've made any progress in getting him to articulate when he feels nervous.

Recently he saw a scene in a movie that scared him, and he told us he was scared. That was a big step forward for him, and he's been very excited lately to tell us when he finds things "spooky" and whether he's "scared" or "not scared". I'd love for him to start doing this with telling us when he's nervous.

Our current plan is just to keep modelling the desired behaviour (e.g. telling him when we're feeling nervous and asking for comfort). I'm hoping to get others' thoughts on this, either from a best practices/ theory perspective or just from other parents who have dealt with similar issues.

Also, just noting that we've discussed this with a psychologist. They assessed him for ADHD and autism, concluded that there were no symptoms, and dumped us. We're in an area where finding another psychologist is not practical.

title: Is ADHD therapy effective?
body:
My daughter is four years old and has a lot of trouble paying attention and sticking with a task (both at home and at preschool). I'm not a doctor but the particular way she gets distracted reminds me so much of myself when I was younger (I was diagnosed with ADD).

In the late 80s and 90s, my parents sent me to child therapists and we went through several medications. We eventually gave up on the medications as even the ones that were effective had side effects that made them not worth it. I asked and my mother said that she doesn't think the therapy was helpful. I just had to develop discipline and work hard to pay attention.

Have therapy/medicine improved a lot since the 90s? Is it worth finding a therapist for my daughter or should we try more "home remedies"?

title: Child doesn't care about being corrected at home but cries for the same reason in kindergarten
body:
I'm not sure if it's normal behaviour or not but my child doesn't mind being corrected at home by me or my wife but if he e.g trampled tulips in the kindergarten garden and the teacher corrects him then he even cried.

I try to convince him that it's actually good that teacher correct him because he knows that it's bad and can stop doing this but there is no reason to cry because of being corrected. It doesn't work.

How should I handle this and is it normal that child doesn't care to much about being corrected by me but overreacts being corrected by teacher?

title: Are window screens (on upper floor) a false sense of security?
body:
My 7-year-old was looking out the window from our bedroom on the second floor last night. I went to the bathroom, heard a noise, came back, and the screen was gone. I asked her, and she said she "high fived the sky" like in Moana. I thought that was such good bullshit, I gave it to her. We looked together and talked and went to bed and left the window open because the air was nice.

My partner came through the room at some point in the night and closed the window, and brought it up with me this morning as a worry. I conceded I should have closed the window because, if one tries, one can easily imagine a hundred ways, however unlikely, that a kid could fall out.

BUT when in comes to putting the screen back in, I am hesitant. Clearly, it pops out super easily. Most of the ways I could imagine a kid falling out of the window would be accidental, and the perception that there is a barrier definitely ameliorates the fear in the mind of my partner. If there is any question at all that a kid might fall out the window, I would rather my child potentially be afraid of the distance to the ground, than to put up a screen that easily pops out.

In any case, I will talk to my kids about windows balconies and falling, and probably put something on the window to stop it from opening beyond the diameter of their heads.

But do you think a flimsy window screen at all reduces the danger of upper floor windows? What do you think of my inclination to leave the screen off because of my partner's perception of danger? Maybe it makes the open window less interesting? Isn't that factor just the novelty, though? Balconies and decks would be more dangerous, right? Anything else?

title: How can I help my little sister. (tw if needed idk the rules/guidelines of this site yet: a bit of childhood trauma dump and 'loud' household)
body:
This is kind of long; the more important stuff is a bit lower down.

mostly back story stuff, not as relevant

Hello, I'm not a mother/father, but I'm the big sibling parent. I love my little sister, and she is literally everything to me. I don't mean to trauma dump/vent, but without her, I might not be here today. However, unlike my mother, I won't make her feel as though she is responsible for my well-being; just keeping her happy and safe is enough.

She's about 2 years old now (turning 3 early summer), and I would like to help her. Other than her usual toddler stuff like tantrums and stubbornness (and I don't mean to sound like every other over-praising parent), she is an amazing little girl. She's smart for her age and learns fast, her day care even says she has the intelligence of some of the 4–5-year-olds there, she even talks smart like them and understands stuff on their level. She even (willingly, don't worry) loves to help out around the house with things like laundry, cleaning, and organizing. She's a strong daredevil; she lifts weights, does pull-ups, flips, and is always climbing and jumping on/off stuff.

I often worry about her safety and well-being, especially since she rarely feels pain. idk all the information, but she was diagnosed with something that makes her more tolerable to pain/feel little to non. There was even a time when her finger got stuck in the gap of her highchair. Her poor finger was smooshed, and she barely cried; she was only upset that she was stuck. I'm absolutely terrified that one day something may happen to her and I won't know because she doesn't have the feeling to tell me if there's anything wrong with her and/or her body.

My mother also yells a lot when there are other ways to deal with things, even as I'm writing, she's been yelling at her for about the past hour or 2. My sister is often crying, and due to my own trauma with her, I'm scared, and I feel guilty and at fault for not helping. I try to take my time to understand and talk to her to give her a safe space, and she almost always listens to me. Even when she's being stubborn/upset, I try to find out what's wrong. Like I said, she's strong, so if she's crying, I know something absolutely terrible is bothering her, and my mother doesn't understand that and thinks she's just causing trouble even tho she's a good kid.

Main topic/what I need help with

Yes, like every other child to every other parent, she causes some stress; all kids do. It's not her fault, and she didn't choose to be like this. My mother is the one who chose to have her, just like I chose to take care of and protect her. I will never blame my sister for nor tell my sister about the harm she causes me. If I were to sacrifice myself and lose an arm, I would never blame her. If she gets sick and needs a kidney or something, I will never blame her for any harm it will have on my body. Because I chose this, I wanted this, not her, so why should she be the one to blame? My mother chose to have her, so why blame her for giving you the responsibility of parenthood?

I want to keep being there for her and help her, try to find some way to make sure she's not affected or as affected as I was as a child, but also in a way that doesn't make my mother angry. She's young, and I don't want to teach her to hate her mother or purposely replace her mother, but instead, protect her from as much as I can and let her know that she can/should be safe and happy without it negatively affecting her. If she decides to be distant or ends up disliking or even hating her later on, that would be on her grounds. If she chooses to love her, I will also accept that, but I also want to let her know that some of the things she does are wrong in a way that doesn't make her mother seem like some monstrous villain.

I also want to learn how to help and teach her. Like what's popular for kids in this generation, how can I communicate/relate to her, what methods/sources can I use to teach and help her while making sure she knows that mistakes are ok, and she can still have fun being a kid, something I was never taught? I want to build a relationship with her, but also don't want to be too strict, but not negligent.

I don't want my own trauma to be the reason she struggles in life. I want to be strict enough to teach her right from wrong, but easy-going enough to make sure she's happy. Unlike my mother, I won't let her know about my problems/make her seem like she's responsible or at fault; I know firsthand how heavy that burden is, especially on a child.

I said before that she's probably the only reason I'm still here today. My mother to told me that but in a way where she told me/made me think that I cause her stress and trigger a seizure and if I wasn't good enough or if something were to happen and she were to end her life it would be my fault and she would always talk to me about her problems like therapist or something. I want my sister to know that I love her and show her how much she means to me instead of burdening her with my mental issues.

I want to support her and her interests/hobbies. I can try to get a job and hide some money to save up for her. I can buy her food, clothes, and toys. Even if it's expensive, I can maybe even take her to the museum that matches her passion, I'll buy tickets to her favorite movie or concert. I'll go on field trips or to amusement parks with her. I want to be there for her. If she wants to be in a band, I'll buy the guitar, if she wants to be an artist, I'll get the brushes, if she wants to be a doctor, she's too young to study it right now but I'm sure as hell going to play Operation with her next family game night.

Please, I'm begging to anyone who may listen, how can I help her, how do I teach her, how do I be there for her? I love her so much, and I want her to have the childhood she deserves, the childhood I never had. I'm a child hidden in the mind of an adult, stuck in the body of a child. I feel that if I help her, the spirit of that hidden child can finally rest peacefully. I'm not doing this for me but for both that child and my sister. Please help me.

title: 9yo not listening and lying
body:
My son is 9yo, we live with my wife brothers, they are below 25 and after 21. Recently my son has stopped listening e.g. he is skipping brushing teeth in night, he doesn’t listen first time, it has to be at least 3 times.

Today what shocked me is that I took him somewhere for playing admission and when ask if there any other classes like cricket to which he said no but there was e.g. other games, so later he claimed he told me but only wanted to get in football and I told him he didn’t. What I know has changed : Right now I don’t have a car because I am paying off debt so I bought kids bicycle and they go to school on it, I have heard my wife complaining that we cannot go anywhere whereas I do get car on rental on special occasion and went on pinic etc but my wife often complain even jokingly about no car which I think is playing with kids mind. Secondly my son started to go with his uncle every weekend on football games, my wife didn’t seek my permission or told me until he wasn’t at home and asked. My opinion is because the guys he is playing or sitting around at game are around 21 and the way young people talk about parents like “old man” etc is playing with my kids mind. Also today when I told my wife that our son won’t go to football with his uncle because of what I think and she convey her the message to the uncle, the uncle was like why? Why your punishing him etc? I can go long stories about how my wife family has to prove everything should be according to them (in my previous post there is a lot of issues) e.g. trying to change my son mind of having haircut of this style or tell him he look strange etc.

Little background is that I have noticed same behaviour on my wife family side where they claim they said it but never did or say something upsetting and claim they didn’t.

I am really worried about the toxic behaviour, I talked with my wife and she is telling me that I am forgetting, I know I don’t because like she and today my son mentioned it, it is like I am having blackouts.

How can I stop this toxic behaviour from my kids as my 9 yo is starting to show the sign of that behaviour seeping in him.

title: How To Handle Daughter's Bathroom (#2) Accident?
body:
Our daughter (ca. 12-13 years old) plays softball for her junior high school team. The other day they played a game where apparently the bathroom facilities weren’t so great. Our daughter claims that the stalls in the bathroom didn’t have doors on them for privacy. She says she urinated there but didn’t go #2. Well, she then had an accident in her pants on the bus riding home from the game.

My husband and I strongly disagree on how to handle this. He picked her up at school after the game. When he found out what happened, he yelled at her quite harshly – apparently telling her that she should be ashamed of herself and telling her that that was inexcusable at her age. I came home from work to find my poor daughter just sitting on the toilet crying.

Now, we both agree, obviously, that she should have used the bathroom at the game. She does have to learn that you can’t always be selective when it comes to what bathrooms you’re willing to use. As the saying goes, when you gotta go you gotta go. But I think she’s already learned that lesson by what happened on the bus coming home after the game. I think if she could go back and do it all over again, she’d do just about anything to avoid messing in her pants on the bus in front of her friends. I see no reason to punish her or even shame her any further over this.

My husband insists that at her age she should have known better and that further punishment is warranted. He says what she did is inexcusable. He says the lack of stall doors is no excuse for her to go in her pants instead. Well, obviously, she should have known better but stuff happens. I seriously doubt she made a conscious decision to go in her pants instead of using the bathroom there. I can’t even remember the last time she went in her pants like this. To me, this is hardly the crime of the century. I say, chalk it up to experience. She suffered the consequences of a bad decision and I seriously doubt she’s ever going to do it again.

title: Daughter Doesn't Want Her Father At Her Softball Games
body:
10 days or so ago, I wrote about my 13 year old daughter having a #2 accident on the bus ride home from one of her softball games. I explained that it happened because she didn't want to use the bathrooms at the game because there were no doors on the individual toilet stalls. My question concerned how her father handled the matter -- specifically, by yelling at her and shaming her for the accident. And he was insisting that she be punished for doing it.

Our daughter was obviously upset about it and I refused to allow my husband to punish her further. I instead helped her clean up the mess and tried to treat it as casually as I could.

I now have a follow-up problem. For the most part, our daughter seems to be coming through the experience just fine. She does seem to be getting over it. However, this has caused a serious rift between her and her father. Last weekend, she told her father that she doesn't want him to come to any more of her games. I was stunned when she told him this. And he was stunned as well. And I was supportive of her when she had the accident, but I don't like this at all. I don't want to flat-out tell her that she can't bar her father from her games, but I don't want this situation to linger. So far, he has honored her request, but I don't know how long we should let this go on.

title: Helping a teen with a difficult team-mate
body:
Background

My 9th grader (14M) is currently at a selective high school which he loves. He's what one would call twice exceptional - quite smart but flakey. So his grades fluctuate between 100s and 0s (missing) with a majority of assignments getting late penalties.

Current Problem

He's in an engineering class, building a contraption with a team mate. He only has a C till now in this class, so getting this final project right is critical for him. He's been working hard, but the team mate is turning out to be a problem. The team mate is constantly being negative, bad vibes, telling my kid not to bring down his grade - and - not working on anything. My kid has never had problems with anyone till now, so I am leaning towards believing my kid.

Need suggestions

There is barely a week to finish the project, what advise would you give my kid to do the best in the bad situation. The teacher is not of much help - as the teacher has seen too much substandard work from my kid (and I do agree that my kid turned in late, rushed, substandard work).

title: How do I tell my strict mom about a boy I really like?
body:
Me and a boy have been talking since October. Recently he asked me to be his girlfriend. I said yes of course. I’ve snuck him over a couple of times but his parents think that my mom is home while he’s over. His parents know all about us and think my mom knows. My mom only knows a little bit about him; she thinks he’s just a friend.

I’m going to confess soon. It kills me that she doesn’t know what I’m doing and that I’m sneaking him over. However, my mom has a no boy policy and she’s not ready for me to be in a relationship with anyone. I feel I’m of age (turning 18 in less than 6 months) and she raised me to be careful of the guys I want to be with. I barely talked to any guys before this one and I think he’s a good guy.

What should I say to her?

title: Car seat transition
body: I found a lot of different answers to this question. But I am hoping for a more solidified response. my son is about to be three years old on July 2 of 2025. He currently weighs 39 pounds and all of the responses on the Internet that I found say he’s capable being put in a booster seat at the age of four or if he weighs 40 to 80 pounds. So I guess my question is is it possible to put him in a booster seat at 40 pounds even though he will probably only be three years old or do I have to wait until he is four years old and keep trying not to pinch his chubby little legs in the five point harness buckles? I live in the state of Pennsylvania if that makes any difference and I drive either a minivan, a small SUV, or a small four-door sedan car.

title: My brother is addicted to video games
body: My little brother is adicted to video games. He is 15 years old. When my parents try to do take his laptop away, he cries and yells at them. It is only getting worse. He stays up late to play these games. He is into Roblox. It is very annoying. What should I do?

title: Party Snub or overreaction?
body:
I am more upset than I want to admit that my child was excluded from another’s birthday party. I am trying to forget it but it’s difficult.

For context my child and the other child play together after school every other day in a friend group of 5. My son and the other child even play on their own as well. The other kids in the friend group all got invites to the block party so of course my son found out and was confused.

We invited them to our birthday parties and he comes every time, I even watched him at other parties so the parents could leave. I am a single parent and I do get isolated more because I can’t attend all social events but it’s feels like we are being excluded on purpose and I don’t know what to do with this sadness and it feels like my fault.

Do I talk to them or just leave it and just focus on my son?

title: How to talk to your child after arguement with spouse
body:
I had a argument with my wife and my 9 yo son witnessed it while my wife was throwing stuff at me. During the fight I stood up and to control her and we fell due to being off balance. This seemed like I hit her when it was actually me falling onto her. Afterwards I her to stand up. My wife wanted me to leave the house (We live with her brothers as they don't have parents), so I did. My wife and I worked out things over a month and I am back in house. During that month I was talking to my kids on phone and meeting them once a week as I was out of the city.

Now I am back I see huge difference in my son. I asked my wife and she told my son that:

It is better to live alone rather than fighting.

Dad is not coming back.

My wife is very emotional and makes decisions based on the situation and not on history. I also know there had been discussions in the house saying I had assaulted her and was not a happy husband. The reason I think this is because I lived with her family long enough to know.

I have talked to my wife about the home environment and for her it is fine to talk about people behind their back, but this is affecting my mental health.

My son is not listening, he is rolling eyes when I ask him to do something like 'get changed and let's go for prayer'. I see a huge difference in his attitude now, I know he is growing apart because of what happened between me and my wife. I think his uncle talked to him and this has changed my son.

Should I ask my son if he has any questions of what happened? I know if his uncle has told him not to ask, he won't. TBH I feel like I am losing hold of my child as he is heavily influenced by his uncle. I would say something 2-3 times, but if his uncle says it once and it is done or even I have to tell him to follow the routine he won't do it but if his uncle tell him, they do.

As a parent what should I do?

title: 3yo won't potty train
body:
My son is 3 and will start school in September. His little brother was born just on May 30th.

We started potty training early may with help from daycare and it actually started getting better at daycare to the point he wasn't having any accident or just small ones for quite a while.

Now at home it was a different story. He kept having accidents every now and then and we started feeling anxious about taking him to the playground or just leaving the house, in case he would just wet (or poop) all over.

We got so stressed with the new baby and all that at some point we gave up momentarily and went back to the diaper, whilst at daycare they kept using underpants and it was going well.

2 weeks ago we restarted the process and it actually was going great, he had a full week with no accidents, but then last Friday he peed on his chair and ever since then he's been constantly having big and small accidents again, even worse than before I'd say.

Throughout this process he would never tell us he needed the potty neither at home or at daycare, but at the latter he would have set times and a routine and he was able to keep it in til it was time I guess.

We are running desperate because it's been 3 months and he isn't really getting consistently better or hasn't let us know before the accident a single time, and school is around the corner... We never scolded him and gave him lots of praise but lately it's been so frustrated I'll admit I've yelled at him a couple of times :(

Any tips for us?

title: Why my kids have 0 interest in studying or doing anything that grows them
body:
I posted a question 5 years ago about my 5yo always watching tv and iPad. He is almost 10 yo now but never ever he want to study on it’s on, no progress in any subject, I got him drone on his birthday but he never flew it and always want something expensive and then it’s sitting on shelves. He watch tv all day or wanna go to park and tv again, as I cancel cable because I couldn’t track what he watches so he watches YT like Mr beasts or Fortnite videos as I have Nintendo switch so they play on them, I have set timer of it but when I don’t, it can be played for 6-8 hours!

Why doesn’t my son has any interest outside of tv, console game or just go to park? My 5yo younger son is following his footsteps and I am worried because he start watching tv after waking up, no teeth brush or face wash until I say or get upset.

Talking to mom she always tell me that home should be relaxed not a timetabled as in army but am I wrong to set things in order because as a father I know how hard lives become later on with wrong habits.

title: Older daughter wetting self
body:
I have a daughter who is 10 years old. After she is done stretching for gymnastics at home, she has a very visible wet spot in the crotch area. There is no laughing when stretching and no stimulation of that area. It has happened a few times now.

Is this normal? School is starting in September and she wants to join the gymnastics team. Should I forbid it so she doesn't get embarrassed?

title: How can I get my three sisters to actually try and win?
body:
My six-year-old sister ask me if we could have a rock wall climbing race on the playground Rockwall. I said yes of course, And she wanted to have a race, so I did racer of the wall like she asked. Every single time though she lost. I know she knows how to climb the rock wall, I was encouraging her to try and climb a little bit faster, but she kept losing every time we would race. How can I get her to climb a little bit faster so she can try to win?

my other sister Riley is 8 and she really wanted to have an arm wrestling contest. And no matter what she never did win. Again I tried to encourage her to give all of her strength, and she says that she was but I didn’t feel much of anything at she was never able to win. So how can I encourage her to use all of her strength so she can try and win?

My younger sister Emily is four and she wanted to have a running race with me on the track that’s on the playground. I have seen Emily run before, but still whenever we raced she never did win. So how can I encourage Emily to run faster so she can try to win?

I (18) was playing with them just like I would with my friends, and I know that all three of them know how to do these activities. So wouldn’t Hannah just need to climb a little bit faster? Riley just get a little bit more strength? And Emily just run a little faster? It seems like they weren’t really trying because I was able to win very very easily.

title: Why kids are unbothered by one parent decision and not with upset with other?
body:
I Told my 9 and 5yo about me going back to my home country and they were totally normal with it but a month back when their mom told them about she is going for 1 week they were nervous and sad so my wife dient go.

This shocked me and I am asking if my kids are less attached to me or don’t care in comparison to my wife.

I don’t remember not being there for my kids but their calmness and unbothered shook me.

title: How do I introduce my 5 yo granddaughter to her father that went to prison when she was 3 months old?
body:
My son and his girlfriend had twin girls 5 years ago. At three months of age one of the twins died from a brain bleed (stroke). My son was arrested that day for the murder of his daughter and has been in prison since on a plea deal from the prosecuting attorney, not wanting to go to a jury trial on a gamble with "12 of his peers" and face life in prison without parole.

My granddaughter has been vetted and approved for phone calls and visitation. She talks with him on the phone, but doesn't understand why she can't be with him now, or even where he is. My son is desperate to see his daughter and to be in her life as her father. His girlfriend has not taken her to visit him, the child wants to see him so I have offered to take her, but I know she will have lots of questions and I want to be ready for them so I can honestly and kindly answer them.

I have stepped in, the only male grandfather/uncle/brother to be a male/father role model for her, so we have a really strong relationship. How best can I make this happen and what can I expect question wise, what is the best way to handle those questions? My son is now 18 months from parole and wants to have established a relation with her prior to release. Any thoughts or ideas appreciated.

title: How do I handle my controlling, emotionally draining, and unpredictable mother at 17 years old?
body:
I'm currently 17 years old but I feel stuck in time. I graduate in less than a year now but I'm honestly nervous to be randomly let go into the world but at the same time, it's what I'm most excited for. I can't wait to leave behind this toxic cycle.

I feel as if every decision I make to have fun and enjoy my final year at home becomes completely criticized and controlled. I have a job and a steady paycheck yet somehow my parents absolutely hate it when I spend even a small amount of my own money. My mom used to tell me to "eat more" and even "spend more money on food" but now she's criticizing me for spending money on "food that disappears in minutes" or clothes. When I have packages arrive at my house and I'm not around, she typically opens it immediately and gets mad. Then my dad will proceed to pull up my bank statements and read them out loud, publicly shaming me for the things I have spent my own money on that I've worked hard to earn.

My parents are also extremely strict with my phone. I currently own what is called a Bark Phone (a fully monitored device that allows parents to easily stalk and see their children's activities). They have to accept every contact, every app, and basically have access to every activity on it. I cannot access Google and all social media besides Instagram. And even Instagram has a 24/7 time limit that is only able to be controlled and opened by my mother. In fact, my phone does not even have a password. If my phone ever gets lost, all someone would have to do is simply swipe up and they can access my entire phone. Additionally, my parents have the ability to lock my entire phone, not even allowing texting or calling anybody, which they frequently resort to when they're mad. Although I appreciate their concerns for my safety, I'm 17 years old and in a committed relationship that I often can't text in without them stalking my messages or taking them out of context. It feels like my parents know more about my own relationships with people than I do and it just seems unfair and like an invasion of my privacy. I cannot have private conversations with anybody. It feels like my mom is almost jealous of my healthy and happy relationship with my boyfriend because she frequently tries to instigate problems with him. I'm also completely unable to vent to my boyfriend and my friends (or anyone else really) about my family situation because it alerts them when I do so, leading them to take my phone away or punish me. She winds up telling me "your boyfriend is going to get sick of your venting and problems and break up with you" or "maybe that's why your old friends left you."

My mom makes me feel as if I have nobody to go to and closes off all possible doors when it comes to talking to somebody about how I feel. She acts like our family business is top secret and not sharable in the slightest. She makes several rude remarks during our conversations that affect me more than she is able to understand. Her words continuously stick with me and cause me to stress and feel emotionally drained. Although this entire notion is pretty much in my mom's control because her and my dad never get along due to their different parenting styles. My mom is so much more controlling than my dad but my dad just learns to obey what she wants because she'll threaten for divorce or begin an argument. Their dynamic together is unhealthy and I've observed they're both separately better parents when they're not around each other but they always stay together.

My parents take my phone every single night before bed even though they make me pay for the phone bill. Thinking that since I'm paying for my phone myself they wouldn't mind, I decided to buy my own phone a few months ago. Once it arrived, my mom got extremely angry and sent it back. I used to have an iPhone and my parents recently claimed they wouldn't mind me using it again but they claimed that they hid it and don't know where it is anymore. Regardless, I just know if I purchased a phone again, they'd be incredibly angry. My mom makes me pay the bill for my insanely monitored phone yet she still calls it "her phone" as if I'm not the one paying for it myself.

My parents constantly change their mind about things and I never know what to expect and how they'll feel on a certain day, making it unpredictable and stressful for me. Example: I told my mom about a hair appointment two weeks in advance and she agreed with it. I reminded her again about two days before and she still said it was alright. But somehow, the day before, she tells me I need to cancel my appointment just to get my brother off the bus.

They also tend to favor my brother a ton. My parents drove me to school every day last year but this year for whatever reason they make me walk because both of them need to be here to simply watch my 11 year old brother get on the bus. (We have two cars by the way). They're always praising him and offering him money, letting him play on his VR headset all day long, they let him cuss, talk back, and a bunch of other things I could never get away with. This is just one example of the many things I've experienced.

On top of all this, my mother body shames me and shames me for my clothing choices, and does it in a completely inappropriate way. I once was wearing a tube top a few months ago and she said "what if somebody did this" and yanked it down until I was shirtless and had to physically cover myself so she wouldn't see my breasts. And TODAY she pulled my shorts up from the bottom till my underwear was showing, claiming it was an "inappropriate" pair of shorts but it wasn't inappropriate until she did that. These are really the only circumstances of her putting her hands on me. Although, I've been told this is sexual harassment but she makes it seem casual and acts like it's her right.

My mom also consistently pressures me about college and scholarships when I'm simply not ready to discuss with her, as I'm trying to enjoy my childhood while it lasts, the childhood I never really got to experience with all the moving and complications we've been through. I do want to go to college but I feel like she's making more decisions in the process than I am myself. This adds tons of stress and pressure onto my back.

I feel like a child in an adult's body and I don't know what to do about it anymore. Continuing to do the things I love just disappoints them and angers them but living by their standards only limits me and what I'm able to do in my life.

Discussing how I feel with my mom especially, even in a polite way, can sometimes cause them to be angry with me or blame me, claiming I love to "play the victim role." Because of the amount of times she's said this, I've convinced myself that my feelings aren't valid and whatever I experience isn't important enough to actually discuss. I often question whether or not I'm the bad guy or if I'm even going through anything serious or just normal. I always underestimate how badly I'm treated by her. After arguments, my mom either doesn't let it go at all and holds a grudge against me, or by the very next day, she's acting like she's my best friend and nothing ever happened. It's so unhealthy and unfair that I never know what to expect or what to do. All I want is to be the daughter that feels wanted and to impress them with everything they hope for but it just doesn't feel possible when they have such a hold on my decisions and lifestyle.

Short disclaimer: I do get along with my parents often. When they’re not in their negative states, they’re extremely funny, fun, and nice to spend time with. I know they love me and understand how much I’ve been through but I just fear that for my age, it’s abnormal the boundaries that are placed on me.

I'd really appreciate any help I can get on how I can maturely address this situation without my parents getting really mad, because if I criticize them at all they won't talk to me for a while.

title: My Son is turning 18 and dresses like he’s still 14
body:
I’ve always been of the mindset that you “dress for the job/life that you want and not the life you have” and it’s served me well throughout my life. I think back to my fashion choices at his age and it was largely event driven and I dressed for the occasion. I work in the Biotech field.

My son is stuck in what seems like skater bros fashion, but doesn’t skate, has grown his hair out long (which I actually love), wears a beanie and graphic T’s of NWA, Ice Cube, Tupac, etc. I know my son has lofty and achievable aspirations and I know it shouldn’t matter, but society dictates what’s acceptable and whether or not you’re taken seriously in the professional world.

He’s not a small man either. He’s a 5’11” big framed gentle giant built like a linebacker. If you didn’t know him, you’d probably be intimidated by him. I know that he’s taken his style cues from his sister who dresses similarly and his girlfriend as well. He’s graduating High School this year and has aspirations for a Juris Doctorate. He does not attend brick and mortar classes; all school is online.

title: How do I help my child avoid getting distracted?
body:

To give an example, sometimes when we send him to his room to get changed into or out of his clothes, when we then check on him 15 minutes later nothing has happened and he is doing something completely unrelated (like reading a book). When we ask him why he is doing something else, his answer is that he got distracted.

He is a smart kid – he already skipped a grade in school and is still following an advanced program – and he occasionally admits to us that he wants to be distracted if he doesn't feel like doing the task that is expected of him. For this reason, it is not an option to take away the things that could cause a distraction, because the biggest of those is his brain.

Does anyone have any tips on how we can help our son to resist the temptation of distractions (i.e., stop wanting to be distracted), especially for tasks/chores that are not what he wants to do at that moment?

title: How to support bodily autonomy in 2 year old daughter during hard tasks

It feels especially bad to power through when she wants us to respect her space, because I think it's so important for her to understand that those words have meaning and should be respected.

How are other folks handling those power struggles, especially with through the lens of trying to let her maximize her sense of self and autonomy?

title: Obese daughter refuses dieting
body:
I'm Arthur. Well, I'm a husband and a father, and truth be told, I'm not entirely sure what to do with my daughter.

Cathy is 14 years old, and has always been overweight. She hasn't developed any other serious health issues as a result of her obesity - yet - but doctors do mention that her weight is a problem on its own, even in absence of other problems. As a result, throughout her life, we - me and my wife - were sometimes trying to fix this: put Cathy on a diet, start her on an exercise regimen, etc. However, and I do admit this is our great failing, we simply don't have enough time for our children. Both me and my wife work long hours. Unfortunately, and tragically, as a result we are both mostly absent from our children's life. So we cannot consistently implement any long-term program. Again, I do understand that this is unacceptable on our part, as parents must be present in their children's lives.

We're trying to remedy this. I quit my second job and negotiated much shorter working hours in my primary job. So I'm hoping to be actually there for my children from now on. After a year and a half, or so, we expect that the situation will reverse - I'll have to take more working hours again, but my wife should become more free instead.

Because of this, I hoped to, among others, finally implement doctors' repeated advise about Cathy and help her lose weight - in a healthy and sustainable way. But, to my surprise, I now faced strong resistance from Cathy herself. It's the first time Cathy takes such a stance - in the past, when told she needed to lose weight, she was usually accepting the necessity, even if grudgingly.

Cathy says that she's fed up with everyone telling her she must shrink. She says she likes being fat, she wants to be fat, she chooses to be fat, she's going to get even fatter. She says she hates being hungry, she loves food and loves being full 24/7. Being full feels awesome, being hungry sucks. And so she consciously chose to eat as much as she pleases, regardless whatever everyone else may be saying. In fact, she decided that for this week she's going to eat as much as she's only able to, and if she likes it, she's going to continue this indefinitely. The only concession she's willing to take is that she may avoid the worst of the junk food and keep moving her body, in order to avoid health failure. But no more.

Indeed, she seems to avoid McDonald's, Coca-Cola and Lay's. She also walks to school and home rather than taking a bus. But... Eh, I think yesterday is a good example of how much she eats:

  • Breakfast: A generous portion of porridge with banana, cherry jam, quite a lot of honey and quite a lot of butter;
  • A second breakfast on her way to school - a sandwich, a pastry, a yogurt, a cup of hot chocolate, all bought from the local bakery;
  • In school, another sandwich, then lunch at the school cafeteria, then another pastry;
  • On her way home, she visited her friend's house, whose grandmother gleefully provided another lunch for both of them;
  • Finally, a salad she prepared for herself for supper: fruit and nuts.

She thinks she eats healthily because hey, she eats fruit, nuts, yogurt and actual lunches, not burgers at McDonald's, and that this somehow makes the pastries, the butter, the meat and the sheer volume of food she consumes more acceptable.

I'm at a loss. What should I do?

title: Vlogging for teen, consequenses and mitigations
body:
My child really likes attention. He likes goofing around entertaining people, he likes to play an instrument for an audience, and he has been asking us for a Youtube account so he can post stuff since he was about 8.

I did not want to do this because I feel I cannot oversee all the consequences. Now he is 12, he has Whatsapp and Whatsapp has Channels which is a little like Youtube. I find it cumbersome that minors can publish videos of themselves without parent's consent, but it is what it is. He really enjoys vlogging but again I think that we do not oversee all the consequences. I see several issues, see below, and I'd like to know if I'm missing some.

  1. Videos that are fun now can be viewed as 'cringe' later, and could be used for bullying him

  2. Videos are almost certainly fed to an AI, and will be used without our consent in ways we cannot forsee, by foreign companies, driven by greed and operating outside the law.

  3. Now the videos are of stuff he does of his own accord, but there is the risk that he could be manipulated or coerced into doing things we do not want him doing. This could be as seemingly harmless as making an ass of himself, showing his ass or doing some dangerous stunt. Or worse.

  4. Making videos also entails watching videos, and the platform invites binge-watching short videos (Whatsapp channels much less so then Youtube or TikTok), an activity that is bad for mood, mental and physical wellbeing in general and eyesight in particular.

The issues can be somewhat mitigated by using another platform. I have looked at Zigazoo (a moderated video pltaform for kids) and Peertube (a host-yourself platform). I fear Zigazoo will not work for him because then his friends (his 'audience') would also need the paid subscription. Peertube is not very popular yet, so I might have to push a little, but it is an option. The videos can still be viewed and saved by random people with bad intentions or be scraped by AI, but they would be less visible.

What other issues am I missing? What options are there to mitigate potentially harmful consequences of vlogging? Having a better understanding myself will help me explain all this to my child.

title: What should I do if I know my son (10) repeatedly searched "Boy dress as a girl" online?
body:
Before seeing that he was searching for this kind of material, I had never even thought about it, nor would I have ever associated him with anything like that. Ever since he was very little, he’s always disliked “girly” things — he never played with dolls, never played pretend cooking, didn’t like the color pink. He was obsessed with toy cars, and in the past couple of years he’s gotten into football video games and loves soccer. All his interests have always been very masculine.

So when I saw his search history, I was really shocked — I couldn’t believe he would be interested in watching those kinds of videos. I saw that he’s searched for this type of video about ten times this month. I don’t dare to ask him about it — or maybe I just don’t know how to. What should I do? Should I ask him directly if he wants to be a girl? Or wants to dress like one? Or is he just simply curious? Because from his behavior and appearance, there’s absolutely no sign of this tendency at all. I really have no one I can talk to about this, and I don’t know what I can do to help him…

Edited to add:

Thank you all for your valuable advice and suggestions. I’m sorry I can’t reply to each of you individually, but I really appreciate every single one of your shares, especially from parents of trans kids and those of you who are currently transgender yourselves. Before this, I honestly felt completely lost and didn’t know how to handle this situation.

I want to say that I have a very close relationship with my child. He shares a lot with me. I also understand that everyone has privacy, so even if he doesn’t tell me something, I don’t see it as a problem. As a parent, I just hope he doesn’t keep his worries and problems all to himself or feel like no one can help him. That has been one of my main concerns. I’ve been thinking that even if he really wants to be a girl, I can help him find professional support as long as he’s willing to talk to me.

Since I made my previous post, I’ve been observing him carefully, and honestly, I haven’t found any sign or indication that he has these worries or tendencies. However, What I can do is make sure he gets a very strong message from us. We love him no matter what, that will never change, and he should always share his unhappiness or worries with us because we will do our very best to help him.

Once again, thank you all. I hope more parents and trans people continue to share your thoughts and experiences. I hope that through everyone’s sharing, more people can understand this issue. Just like me.

title: How to train young teen to fess up and man up
body:
My 12 year old cannot stand to make mistakes. This has been a theme with him his whole life but at this age when kids make more mistakes, I feel it is a bigger issue. Because he does make mistakes but he lies when he is caught even when caught in the act, even after he has been punished. Since he keeps lying after he has been punished it is not (just) strategic lying to avoid punishment.

Example: he threw fireworks out our window with a friend. I yelled at them both and send them downstairs to clean it up. In the garden his dad, who took the garden hose to extinguish the smouldering mess, scolded him in front of his friend and spreyed him wet with the hose in the front of our house. This made an impression.

But still he made up an elaborate story, to make this an accident. He said he picked up some spent fireworks from the street, and put it in his pocket. In his room he took it out and his friend threw put it on the roof. And there it tumbled down and reignited. We know this is untrue: I saw the burning thing fall down as I was looking out, and the friend told his mom that my son had set it on fire and thrown it out.

Like I said this has been a theme his whole life. In school the teachers that liked him the most would take him apart and try to explain to him that it is OK to make mistakes. They have literally told him this with one of us present so we would confirm it to him. We are not particularly strict. The punishment at our house is not so terrible and it is often absent. We do explain why something is forbidden.

This has to do with pride. When he was maybe 2.5 or 3, I remember I tried to explain the concept of making up to him after a tantrum. I tried to tell him even grownups can be very angry at each other, but they can make up and then they shake hands. He looked at me in horror, threw himself on the couch and put his hands under his belly to prevent us from shaking hands.

In the past years things have been going smoothly, so I was not aware we were still dealing with this problem. But now with the lying I think it is very important to teach him that it is OK to make mistakes and to train him to man up to what he does. But how?

title: Giving prizes for not being late to school
body:
TLDR: I plan to start giving prizes for my children for being on time at school - what can possibly go wrong? (it's not as bad I think, bear with me)

Situation

  • I have 2 children, 7 yo and 9 yo.
  • We commute to school. We have option of car or public transport. (Bicycle is an option in better weather, assume it is outside of scope for this question)
  • Children prefer car, I prefer public transport (personal reasons)
  • Children are often late to school. My attempts at changing it made me feel I am the only person at home who cares about being on time and were generally costly (in terms of time, energy, peace at home vs achieved results)
  • Children want to have some collectible cards that are currently popular at school.

What I want to achieve

  • I want children to be on time at school
  • I want children to be aware of time ("do I have a time now to do XYZ or do I need to hurry up?")
  • I want us usually to commute by public transport (secondary priority)

How I plan to achieve it

I plan to buy some of the cards (30ish for initial roll-out). I will introduce a rule that every day that we go to school with public transport AND are on time, children get 1 card at random (shared or 1 each - undecided yet).

I think it should be helpful, because:

  • plan is simple, sufficiently ambitious, achievable.
  • even if it doesn't work fully, it will provide incentive in right direction

Expected problems (please comment on those)

  • I fear children could learn that without prize they have NO reason to be on time (main concern)
  • If I give them 1 card each, it may appear that 1 is worse than another due to random draw
  • If I give them 1 card to share, what happens when 1 is not going to school (e.g. because is sick)?
  • It is possible that on a given day only 1 child is difficult, but both share success or failure.

What are your thoughts? Is this a good idea? Are there problems that I didn't anticipate? How to fix those I did?

In short: how to make it work well?
