title: 7-year-old struggling with German in Germany, limited family language support, how can we help effectively?
body:
We live in Germany and have been here for about 10 years. We are originally from India. At home we speak Hindi and English. My wife and I did not actively learn German in the first years because basic German plus English was enough for daily life.

Now our 7-year-old son is struggling with German at school. His main challenges are:

  • Pronunciation
  • Dictation and spelling
  • Speaking German confidently
  • General anxiety or fear around using German

At home, we have always spoken English and Hindi fluently. We rarely used German with him during his early years. Recently, I started learning German myself, and I noticed that he sometimes sits with me and writes German words. However, he still does not like speaking German with me. I wonder if this is because:

I sometimes correct my own German mistakes in front of him

  • For 7 years, we never expected German from him at home
  • He associates German mainly with school pressure

We hired a university student as a tutor. She has a good bond with him. They read, write, and practice pronunciation together, and she also plays with him. That seems helpful, but progress is slow.

Socially, he mainly interacts with children at school and daycare. We have limited social gatherings, partly due to the weather and partly because our close circle is English-speaking. Most of his free time is spent at home with us, watching TV or playing.

Recently, I noticed that he prefers playing with younger children rather than peers his age. He sometimes puts in minimal effort to learn the language and hopes to “just pass.” Is it happening due to his slow pace of learning? Is it connected to me, as I am learning German after 10 years, still at an intermediate level?

His academic performance is starting to be affected. If he does not meet the language requirement, he may not be promoted

We do not want to pressure him too much and make him dislike studying. At the same time, the situation is becoming serious. Last year, his class teacher suggested that we repeat class 1 for him, but we believed that repeating a class might demotivate him from learning, as he is also emotional.

  1. How can we realistically support a 7-year-old in learning the local language when the parents are not fluent themselves?
  2. How can we increase his confidence in speaking German without increasing anxiety?
  3. Should we introduce more German at home, or is that counterproductive if our own German is imperfect?
  4. Are there evidence-based strategies for helping children in bilingual or late-immersion situations like this?

We are looking for practical, structured advice that balances academic needs with emotional well-being.

title: Is this normal behavior for child and grandparent
body:
I have a 4 year old son who shows extremely strong attachment to his grandmother. And in a normal situation I would applaud such connection, however this expresses itself in unhealthy ways. It symptomatically shows up as him crying for grandmother when she’s not around, undermining us parents hence we set a boundary or rule saying grandma does it this way, or if grandma is around child runs to her for comfort or to escape consequence.

a little background I lived with my mother while he was a baby and I was finishing graduate school. This included long hours of studying and internship where she was the main caregiver, however the last 2 years I have been consistently back and involved in his life. Grandma only watches him one day a week and he attends preschool 3 half days (that is when I get a majority of my work done).

The main issue I encounter is that grandma has a different permissive parenting style where our rules as parents is overridden constantly. This can be anything from food, nap times, behavior/etiquette/manners to spoiling with toys and outings. He is not reprimanded for yelling or demanding things while I am urging him to be polite. I also believe in sleep training and that he should sleep in his own bedroom. For this, I am shamed for exercising an authoritative parenting style being called “abusive” and “cruel”. The worst part is that we still live with grandma (because building my practice has been a slow and painful process due to her lack of support and demands extra funds for “babysitting”) and he refuses to sleep in his room unless she is with him or she constantly tries to bring him in her room to sleep with her. She definitely has some major narcissistic traits and I am noticing co-dependency issues with my son..

Thank God me and my partner just bought a house and will be moved in by the end of the month, but grandma is acting like it’s the end of the world (after all she’s done and sacrificed, everyone is abandoning her) and is adamant that we stop sending him to preschool and that she watch him instead..

Honestly, I think she’s a malignant narcissist and is using my son to stroke her ego and create a power play since I’ve wised up to her gaslighting antics and don’t believe a word she says.

But naturally I want to gather a few outside opinions and see what other parents feel. This will decide If we completely burn the bridge and cut off grandma entirely, or if we allow her to visit occasionally but only with us all present. It sounds horrible cutting her off entirely, but I’m feeling like we have no other choice since she refuses to respect my parenting rules and choices and co-parent responsibly.

title: My youngest's new appearance is triggering, based on the reputation of the eldest
body:
So, that title is not overly explanatory. To expand:

My eldest son has created an incredibly bad reputation for himself over the past 2 years. He had started skipping classes, leaving school grounds, was almost expelled for joining in with his friends that were throwing a large hunting knife at a tree on school grounds, and was finally pulled out of the school due to accusations of sexual harassment of another student (he-said-she-said situation, but profiling was obviously swayed against him). We have transferred him to a new school, which is far more strict and responsive to truancy, yet he is still choosing to skip class (leaving school grounds is a lot harder).

He has also become more emotional/depressed, and has withdrawn from us for help - opting to talk to his aunts/uncles, who then immediately refer him back to us, or fill us in so that we can understand and approach the situation ourselves. This behavior has also involved scratching himself with blades like pencil sharpeners (he has not cut himself - it's only skin deep - it has become apparent this is very much for attention; he does not have a tolerance for pain).

The last part is obviously more normal for a 14/15 year old, however, regardless of our efforts, he still chooses to reject us and our help. We have also been taking him to therapy, which he has accepted and engaged in, but we are still overcoming the fallout of the behavior.

Now, my youngest son has adopted a similar appearance with his hair - wearing it exactly the same way as his older brother (combed down over his face to hide his eyes). He has said "it's just how I like it", which I can understand. Personally, I don't think it looks any good - I had similar conversations with my other son when he started doing it.

The main issue however is that it has triggered some strong emotions in me just by seeing it; it brings up the stress and struggles that we have been through with his older brother. I'm concerned that he is copying his brother's appearance, because he idolizes him, or that he is in a similar situation at his school (we put him in a different school to his older brother due to the issues we were facing there). I obviously don't want him to fall into the same patterns and behaviors as dealing with that once had a severe impact on everyone in the family.

I'm at a stand still on how to approach this - I don't want to suppress my son's self-expression of who he is, but I also can't ignore how I am feeling, why I am feeling the way I do - the cause and potential impact. I know that dealing with it is something I need to do myself apart from this, but I do also want to express my concerns and help them (potentially both) to understand why I feel the way I do.

title: Are there any issues with trading responsibilities for privileges?
body:
My wife and I have used a positive discipline approach for the majority of our children's lives. We don't really punish them, when they do something silly or anti-social we use it as an opportunity to explain better behavior. Basically we don't make them feel bad, we explain and model what the appropriate behavior is. This approach has been pretty successful, they both have strong self-regulation and social skills now.

But now we seem to be in a new era where they know they can break a rule and nothing bad will happen. I'm not too worried about that, but I feel like we're moving into new territory where there needs to be firmer repercussions for their actions.

I've already thought about this, and even asked a similar question a few years ago. The only approach that makes sense to me (that aligns with positive discipline) is to explain to them that they have certain responsibilities that they have to fulfill, and if they don't fulfill those responsibilities then there may be a loss of privileges.

For example, 'your responsibility is to keep your glasses safe', if they end up broken we're going to have to use some of your allowance to pay for the replacement. We don't say it in a harsh or demeaning way, we just explain the reality to them and let the consequence be the consequence. Maybe they screw up and we give them a little bit of leeway to build rapport.

At this time our boys are 4 and 6, although I used the adolescent tag because I'm interested in answers that span the rest of their childhood.

My question is: is this approach basically sound? I can't really envision any other way for positive discipline to work once they're out of the baby stage. And are there any gotchas or alternative approaches that might be worth considering?

title: Is there a recommended method of introducing letter sounds to a four year old?
body:
I've been thinking about literacy concepts for one of my children and trying to understand how we can continue to broaden his horizons. At this point I'm of the opinion that it's too early to push it, but we do read to him a lot, have introduced letter concepts (mostly with his name), and have had him trace letters in workbooks from time to time. He doesn't seem to have a firm grasp of what letters are yet (which I figure is age appropriate). We're keeping it casual at this age because I don't think pressure is going to do anything positive for him.

All of that being said, are there appropriate, recommended guidelines for introducing letters and letter sounds at this age? If it's too early (he just turned four), at what point would it be appropriate to to introduce a minimal amount of structure? And what would that structure look like?

ETA: I'm wondering if this question may be too difficult to answer. I've been researching the topic for a few weeks and am struggling to find anything like a recommended framework. I'm mostly getting various opinions. Some recommend focusing on letter sounds and not names, others recommend focusing on names as well.

From what I can gather the more critical part is going to be introducing these concepts to our son while keeping things fun and not pressuring him. Being encouraging and not too rigid.

title: How do I move forward with my overbearing mom?
body:
I'm 15 and feel super trapped. My mom tracks me at all times, randomly goes through my phone, and searches my room and bed while I'm in it.

The tracking I understand because she wants me to be safe, but whenever the app is wrong it's my fault for not being where I'm supposed to be even if I am.

I also understand that as a teenager digital privacy isn't something I get the privilege of, but I think that if my parents have decided to trust me with a phone then they should embrace it. I have zero access to the internet and very limited apps with no social media. My contacts are constantly monitored and viewed by her and have to be kept up to her standards. Whenever I do something "wrong" my phone is the first thing to go. It has super strict time restrictions and even in the allowed time I have to use it (7am-9pm) it will get taken throughout the day. She has rules like no phones in rooms and they're only allowed in public spaces, but our backyard doesn't count and all of my calls are listened to.

She has searched my bed multiple times and many while I was in it. This one time it was around 2am and she was super convinced that I had my phone in my bed and proceeded to pat me down,turn on all of the lights, throw back the sheets, and turn over my pillows. My phone had been turned in on the family desk where it was supposed to be, but she couldn't find it and immediately jumped to the worst case scenario.

Whenever she gets a feeling that I've done something wrong she'll check my phone and inevitably find something she doesn't like. How do I tell her that if she keeps looking for it she's gonna find it?

This isn't even all of it, she hates my boyfriend and is convinced that all of my friends are keeping stuff about me from her. I've never failed a drug test, I'm in band, getting straight A's, and am thinking about colleges and my PhD. I don't know what else she wants from me. I have a relatively good relationship with my mom on good days and my dad couldn't care less about my phone or boyfriend. He's had to warn me when she comes home and my boyfriend's over and has had to physically stop her from lashing out at me.

I am very grateful that I have 2 parents who care about me, but she's so overbearing and I can't make mistakes or learn from them without it being constantly monitored or intervened on.

title: Can it make sense to pay a child to learn a skill?
body:
I'll caveat this question with the fact that my family is very much opposed to rewards and positive reinforcement. We try to praise only the effort and never tie financial incentives to anything, especially results.

That being said we've discovered that the elementary school our children are attending no longer teach the students to touch type on a keyboard, and that is absolutely a skill that we want them to have. Being able to type quickly on a real keyboard will have huge returns for them over the course of their lifetimes.

Starting with the assumption that we start out teaching them to type with no financial incentive at all and see how it goes / how their intrinsic motivation is, and the second assumption that if they need extrinsic motivation (payment) we don't tie that to results, but just say - you practice for 30 minutes and we'll give you (for example) 5 dollars, and we explain to them why we're doing it this way (typing is important). Could that work? Do you see any downsides to this approach?

title: Word lists: Dolch 200+95 and Fry 200 - used up to which grades in USA schools?
body:
Edward Dolch's list of 220 non-nouns plus 95 nouns (gathered from three other lists in 1936) is used up to which grade in USA schools? And what about Edward Fry's "200" list, meaning his first two lists each of 100 words - what grade are they used up to?

I am interested in the grades at which school pupils in the USA are expected to be able to read all of the Dolch 220+95 and all of the Fry 200. I couldn't find a good source with this info. I realise the ages probably vary, but I'm just looking for a rough answer, which I think may possibly be 3rd grade (D 220+95) and 2nd grade (F 200).

title: 11 year old asked random people for money to buy fish for his new aquarium - how to teach him that this is not ok?
body:
My kid (11) and partner went to an event this weekend and when they came home, my partner told me that during this event, our kid apparently started asking people for money to fund fish for his new aquarium. Apparently, he got close to 80€. And my partner only became aware after around 40€ were already collected, and was baffled by this and did not really know how to deal with it, so it went on. Apparently he (the kid) was not pushy or anything, just his normal charming self (unlike me, kid is a people person). Most people at the event were either friends, friends of friends or acquaintances.

A bit of background: the birthday was 2 weeks and we gifted him an aquarium (which does not exist yet as we were away too much for the summer to really start with the process).

I am a bit mortified that he did that, as, while not rich are sufficiently well off to pay for all the fish we want, albeit we said that we are not going to buy the most expensive fish due to this being the first aquarium he ever had, and also because I want him to know that one does not have to always buy the most expensive stuff. So what probably happend is that he got money from people that might not be as well off as we are. I also wonder what these people will now think of us, because our kid runs around "begging" for money.

This is the first time anything like this ever happened, and if I could I would give the money back, but I (and neither my partner) don't know from whom the money came from. But I definitely do not want this to happen again. What are good ways to deal with something like this? Should we donate the money for a good cause? I feel like if he gets to keep it, there is little to be learned.

title: My son is in a kindergarten with much younger kids - what are my options?
body:
My son is 4 years old. In my town, there are only two kindergartens for children 3-6 years old. So 3-4 yo children go to kindergarten 1 and 5-6 yo children go to kindergarten 2, and the 4-5 yo children are split between the two by their age. My son went to kindergarten 1 last year, and this year he was assigned to the same kindergarten.

Most children in kindergarten 1 are much younger than him, both biologically and mentally. He says he is very bored and does not have friends to play with (most friends he had last year moved to kindergarten 2). Also, the stories and materials taught in the kindergarten are the same as last year, which adds to his boredom. He tells me each day "I do not want to go to kindergarten". Yesterday he told me "today I wanted to run away from the kindergarten, as I was tired from the plays, but I overcame myself".

I asked the managers several times to move him to kindergarten 2, but they said it is not possible due to capacity constraints. The ideal solution would be to open kindergarten 3 for children 4-5 years old, but this is not possible due to the town budget constraints.

I tried to encourage my son to behave as a "big brother" to the younger kids: teach them things that he knows, help them play the games, etc., but he did not seem very interested in this.

What other options do I have, that would make the kindergarten visits more enjoyable and meaningful for my son?

title: How do I know when babies can go over bed guards?
body:
My twin babies (9.5 months old) sleep in my bed. I have placed a mesh bed guard (this type) on all four sides, screwed into the bed frame.

Two nights ago, they discovered a new game: climbing up the guards. They grab the upper edge and use a combination of pull-ups and bracing their feet against the mesh to go up. They can now go at least as far up as to bite the edge from above (I see the spit marks), and the feet come up almost 20 cm above the mattress.

On the one hand, I want to think that they are still safe. They don't the upper body strength to do a very high pull up, and bracing the legs becomes more difficult the higher the legs are. I don't think I could climb over a scaled-up guard myself (although maybe I can? I don't have the opportunity to test). And the official wisdom is that these guards are safe until they reach to the baby's armpits (currently, the babies are 72-ish cm tall and the rails are 67).

On the other hand, I still feel quite worried when I see them go that high after only two evenings of exercising. They are very advanced in motor development. Also, they are underweight (around 7.5 kg), which seems to help them in any activity where their muscles have to carry their weight.

How do I recognize when they are advanced enough to be able to climb over the guard?

title: How do you explain your strong desire to have the baby sleep with you to your wife?
body:
I have the strong desire to house our infants sleeping arrangements in the master bedroom where me and my wife sleep. I'm not talking about in the bed, in a cot next to the bed. I don't exactly know how to explain the reasons why into words. I just have the strong desire to have the baby close to me when I sleep.

Off course I'm not talking about teenagers. I'm Ok for the child to go to his own space as he grows into a toddler, but for the first little while I have the need to have the baby close to me when I sleep. Is this desire natural?

I hope I'm not being selfish and I hope I could discuss this with my wife in an easy way. I keep on seeing people talk about baby monitors for when the baby start crying, but I cannot do it like that. If the baby cries I need to know about it because he should be close to me. I don't know if other people have felt like this?

This has awaken something quite visceral or primal in me. I feel the strong urge to have the baby close to me for about the first year of it's life. I have spent my life in a series of rational academic pursuits but now that parenting is possible I seem to have awaken the lizard part of my brain. I hope some people could relate. I feel like I'm a Vulcan experiencing Pon Farr for the first time.

title: Tell a teen why Private Browsing is turned off, yes or no?
body:
Is it better to be completely upfront and tell a teenager (13) I changed the browser settings on their laptop to make it possible to keep track of their online activities, or to handle this in another way? For example by changing the settings quietly or even not changing the settings and keep track of their online activities in some other way?

The first option is honest but risks creating a conflict for nothing. The second option bypasses conflict, but is sneaky and not the kind of example I want to set.

Other options like periodic history checks are a lot more hassle and again beg the question: out in the open or after hours?

Related questions here and here.

Technical background: My child has a Macbook (for school) with Screen Time and I have parental controls with my iPad. When he uses private browsing I cannot see which websites he visited.
